Tbe above statement is incorrect. The consignees ot the þÿ Albert Horn" applying to the Authorities for permission for the steamer to sail between St. Croix and St. Thomas on the same conditions as those under which Danish vessels trade between the Islands, received an answer, that foreign vessels bcinir, as in most other countries, excluded from tbe coasting trade by tbe existing navigation laws, permission could not be granted to the vessel in question to carry goods or freight hut that & lie would tie allowed to sail lietween the Islands, provided she only carried passengers, in which ease the ship and port-charges would be so trifling as not to warrant any concessions in that respect. When to tbe above is added, that those interested in tbe "Albert Horn" might hy placing her under the Danish Flag, Secure all the advantages required, it will be evident that tbe cause of the attempt to establish steam communication between the Islands not succeeding, lies deeper, than in any Act of the Authorities.

We publish the foregoing communication with much satisfaction as it is at all times our wish to be corrected in every case where we are þÿ incorþÿrect. A few further remarks in addition to what we stated in our article of the 9th instant we shall make, and then leave it to our readers

to determine for us our precise position on the point It was positively known to the Authorities that the steamer for which the concessions were asked sailed under the American flag, and we cannot doubt that it was further known, that by the navigation laws of the United States uo American vessel, once changing her nationality, can ever again sail under her original colours. Now, as the concessions asked for were only for an experimental term of one month or so, it is hardly to he supposed that a vessel of the Albert þÿHorn value, s could venture to change her flag, and failing to be sold in these seas (which in the very face ol the enterprise was most doubtful) sacrifice all her chances of returning to the LLiited Slates, where, under every circumstance, she will continue to retain a ceitain value Let us however suppose that the Albert Horn, with that shrewdutss common to her nation, (yet contrary to þÿ the general belief) had secured a brisk aud thriving þÿtrade between the two Islands during the period of trial, is it not too evident at the same time that the period being limited to a mouth or so, it was in the power of the Authorities to terminate it, whilst ou the other hand the inhabitants of both places would have been afforded the chances of forming an opinion with regard to the success or unsuccess þÿ which, had it beeu favourable, there is little doubt an association would have been formed, the steamer purchased, and her flag forthwith changed. As regards the vessel being þÿ allowed

i to sail between the two Islands, provided she only I carried passengers, in which case the ship and port charges would he so þÿtrifling, we are at. a loss to comprehend what need would there have been to ask the Authorities in order to do that. As things now stand we arc as wise as ever, confirming what a great many people say, that our wisdom teeth have yet to he cut. Evidences are uot wanted to prove that Governments in general possess the power to ameliorate laws, or temporarily suspend them, wherever the cases in point justify such a course. During the Crimean war circumstances made it that British, French, American, and transports of every nation were found indiscriminately mixed up on the sea, employed one way or another, and wherever such exigencies conflicted with international laws, an þÿ order in þÿCouncil from one or other of the nations, subject to being revoked, usually put at rest the objectionable points. When the project was accepted as being a very good one, could not something of this kind have been done? þÿ Ed. Tin.

Immigrants and Liberated Africans. þÿ The number of immigrants and liberated Africans introduced into the West Indian colonies and into the Mauritius during the past year is 30,910. Of this number the West Indies took 9,490, aud the Mauritius 21,484. The return from the Mauritius is only for half a year so that if the same ratio is kept up throughout the year it would give a total of 42,968. All the Mauritian immigrants came from the East Indies, while only 7,719 from that country emigrated to the West Indies. The remaining West Indian immigrants were 699 from China, 1,048 from Madeira, 4 from St. Helena, and 26 from Havana. The return, when compared with that of 1858 shows an enormous increase, and one very much in excess of former years. The numbers for 1858 were as follows: þÿ 5,947 immigrants to the West Indies, and 29,946 to the Mauritius. The increase is entirely attributable to the Coolies from India, who are evidently beginning to appreciate the advantages which are held out to them in the West Indies and the Mauritius. It is to be hoped that this great supply will have a beneficial effect upon the West Indian negroes, by destroying their monopoly cf labour, and by afford- 1 ing the planters another market for supplying their wants.

MACAULAY ON DEMOCRACY. curious letter from lord macaulat on american institutions and prospects. ( From the Southern Literary Messenger ) The following letter we have been permitted to present to the American people, in the pages of the Messenger. It belongs to an occasional correspondence, of some years standing between LordMacaulay and Hon. Henry S. Randall of New York, author of the Life of Jefferson : þÿ Holly Lodge, Kensington, London, Henry S. Randall, Esq. þÿ May Dear Sir, Si, 1857. þÿ You are surprised to learn that I have not a high opinion of Mr. Jefferson, and I am surprised at your surprise. I am certain that I never wrote a line, and that I never, in Parliament, in conversation, or even on the hustings þÿ a place where it is the fashion to court the populace uttered a word indicating an þÿ opinion that the supreme authority in a State ought to he intrusted to the majority of citizens told by the head: in other words to the poorest and most ignorant part of society. 1 have long been convinced that institutions purely democratic must, sooner or later, destroy liberty, or civilization, or both. In Europe where the population is dense, the effect of such institutions would be almost instantaneous. What happened lately in France is an example. In 1848 a pure Democracy was established there. During a short time there was reason to expect a general spoliation, a national bankruptcy, a new partition of the soil, a maximum of prices, a ruinous load of taxation laid on the rich for the purpose of supporting

the poor in idleness. Such a system would, in twenty yetrs, have made France as poor and barbarous as France of the Carlovingians. Happily the danger Was averted ; and now there is a despotism, a silent tribune, an enslaved Press. Liberty is gone; but civilization has been saved. I have not the smallest doubt that, if we hail a purely Democratic Government here, the effect would be the same. Either the poor would plunder the rich, and civilization would perish; or order and property would be saved by a strong military government, and Libert) would perish. You may think that your country enjoys an exemption from these evils. I will frankly own to you that I am of a very different opinion. Your fate I believe to be certain, though it is deferred by a physical cause. As long as you have a boundless extent of fertile and unoccupied land, your laboring population will be far more at ease than the laboring population of the old world; and, while that is the case, the Jeffersonian policy may continue to exist without causing any fatal calamity. Rut the time will come when New England will be as thickly peopled as Old England. Wages will be as low, and will fluctuate as much with you as with us. You will have your Manchesters and Rirminghams; and, in those Manchesters and Birmingbams hundreds of thosands of artisans will assuredly be sometimes out of work. Then your institutions will be fairly brought to the test. Distress everywhere makes the laborer mutinous and discontented, and inclines him to

listen with eagerness to agitators who tell him that it is a monstrous iniquity that one man should have a million while another cannot get a full meal. In bad years there is plenty of grumbling here, and sometimes a little rioting. But it matters little. For here the sufferers are not the rulers. The supreme power is

Ss?« PjU A » II in the hands of a class, numerous indeed but select, of an educated class, of a class which is and knows itself to be, deeply interested in the security of property and the maintenance of order. Accordingly, the malcontents are firmly, vet gently, restrained. The bad time is got over without robbing the wealthy to relieve the indigent. The springs of national prosperity soon begin to flow again: work is plentiful; wages rise, and all is tranquility and cheerfulness. I have seen England pass three or four times through such critical seasons as I have described. Through such seasons the United States will have to pass in the course of the next century, it not of this. How will you pass through them? I heartily wish you a good deliverance. But my reason and my wishes are at war, and I cannot help foreboding the worst. It is quite plain that your Government will never lie able to restrain a distressed and discontented majority. For with you the Majority is the Government, and has the rich, who are always a minority, absolutely at its mercy. The day will come when, in the State of New York, a multitude of people, none of whom has had to more than half a breakfast, or expects have more than half a dinner, will choose a Legislature. Js it possible to doubt what sort of Legislature will be chosen? ( In one side is a statesman preaching patience, respect tor vested rights, strict observance of public faith. On the other is a demagogue ranting about the tyranny of capitalists and usurers, and

asking why anybody should be permitted to drink champagne and ride in a carriage, while thousands of honest folks are in want of necessaries. Which of the two candidates is likely to be preferred by a working man who hears his children cry for more bread? 1 seriously apprehend that you will, in some such season of adversity as I have described, do things which will prevent prosperity front returning; that you will act like people would, in a year of scarcity, devour all the seed-corn, and thus make the next year, a year not of scarcity, but of absolute famine. There will be I fear spoliation. The spoliation will increase the distress. The distress will produce fresh spoliation. There is nothing to stay you. Your Constitution is all sail and no anchor. As I said before, when a society has entered on this downward progress, either civilization or liberty must perish. Either some Casser or Napoleon will seize the reins of government with a strong band ; or your Republic will be as fearfully plundered and laid waste by barbarians in the twentieth century as the Roman Empire was in the fifth ; with this difference, that the Huns and Vandals, who ravaged the Roman Empire, came from without, and that your Huns and Vandals will have been engendered within your country by your own institutions, Thinking thus of course, I cannot reckon Jefferson among the benefactors of mankind ; I readily admit that his intentions were good arul his abililies considerable. Odious stories have been

circulated about his private life ; but I do not know on what evidence those stories rest ; and I think it probable that they are false or monstrously exaggerated. I have no doubt that I shall derive both pleasure and information from your account of him. I have the honor to be dear Sir, Your faithful Servant, T. B. MACAULAY.

COOLIE IMMIGRATION INTO TRINIDAD. The following is an extract from the pamphlet published by llie Rev. Mr. Underbill, of whose tour through the West Indies we have made mention in our Summary. Mr. Underbill is now in Jamaica, and his observations upon the labour question in connection with that island are looked for with much interest. The remarks reproduced in the present extract refer entirely to Trinidad. That the employment of immigrant labour has augmented production, none in his senses would attempt to deny; but if the native peasantry had withdrawn from cane cultivation to the extent some parties would have it believed, the crops would have remained stationary, or shown but a trifling increase. The entire number of immigrants imported into Trinidad, from February 1845 to March 1858, was under 13,000, at a cost of £150,568, for their introduction alone which does not represent, by a considerable sum, the whole expenditure. Not a fourth part of this total amount has been paid by the planters, who have therefore bought their alledged prosperity at the expense of the community. extract. "There remains but one other subject to notice þÿ the effect of the Coolie immigration on the prospects of the negro population. Singularly enough, contrary to the usual expectation, it has improved the condition of the negroes. True, the negroes are no longer the chief dependence of the planter for the production of sugar. On the 158 sugar estates of the island, the field-work is

almost entirely performed by Coolies. The command of Coolie labour enjoyed by the planter has increased the growth of the sugar-cane, and induced the extension of sugar cultivation. With this there has necessarily arisen a demand for hedges and ditches for drainage for carpenters, coopers, enginemcn, boilermen, mule drivers, lumberers, and clearances of forest land. The demand for ground provisions to supply the wants of the Coolie labourers has increased, and the cattle employed on the estates must be fed. There is therefore, a great demand for skilled labour, and for labour of a more remunerative kind than that of the cane-field. The garden produce finds a better market. All these occupations and duties are being rapidly taken up by the negro. He is removed from the position of a mere servitor, and is paid better for the exertions he puts forth. The Coolie is therefore no competitor with the negro in the labour market, and no ill feeling exists because of the displacement of the one by the other. Coolie labour opens a wider field of exertion to the negro, and he is rapidly becoming the artisan and skilled labourer of the Trinidad community. "This interesting and important result could only have taken place in a country where the amount of labour accessible was far below the wants of the community. But it must be a cause of gratulation to the friends of the African race, that in this instance a system which at first sight seemed calculated to lower the rate of- wages, and to de-

prive the negro of the market for his labour, to which he had a right to look for employment, has resulted in his advantage, and in opening to him sources of remunerative employment, which, as a mere agriculturist tied to the soil, he never could have realized. His position is improved, and there is required of him higher forms of labour than can be executed by the cutlass or hoe." þÿ Anti Slavery Reporter for April.

Editor, Circumstances have recently made me acquainted with the surprising fact that the Clerk of the Lutheran Church in this town claims for a person " having died in town and been interred in the country," "grave digger's fee" $C 10 and for " Inviter's fee, a general invitatic«i having been circulated by an unconcerned person" "8 00

$14 40 This claim is propounded, as he says, under the sanction of law, in an instance in which he not only did nothing but in which his services were no way required. There was no grave dug ; for the, body was placed m a vault in the country. The deceased had been my guest, and the invitations were issued solely by me through the sexton of iny Church as my official representative. As a similar claim is likely to occur on the death of a very large proportion of the inhabitants of this island, I propose very briefly to consider the character of the enactment under which it is made. It is unjust. For it gives to au individual payment, tor services he does not. render. Its equity would lie equaled by a law requiring that every article of domestic utility I might need should be purchased at a particular store,

s T & B o I X A V I S, aud that in the event of my purchasing elsewhere any thing of the kind, I must pay that one particular store the price affixed in its (invariable schedule Throughout my life I have paid only for services rendered or for goods for which I have contracted. It is strange that now, under circumstances which should be exceptional, if ever any are, I am asked to pay largely for that for which neither services nor goods have been obtained. "The laborer is worthy of his hire but where one does not I labor and is not asked to labor, why should '' hire" he given to him ? Would our planters be willing to pay laborers whom they had not I employed ? Surely a death in the family is sufficiently j afflictive. All right-minded citizens, when such a calamity occurs, do what they can to soothe and comfort the mourners They endeavor, as far as they are able to " bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." But, it seems, there is one man in the community empowered to aggravate the woe of the sufferers and to add heavy charges to their burdens. In other words, when the kind-hearted and considerate are seeking to ailay grief, he can and does step into the house ol mourning and say, substantially, li re is another weight in the scale ol your sorrows Your loss is great : but you must add in my bill before you can know its full extent. This looks much more like the vinegar and gall offered to the blessed Saviour than the oil and wine of the good Samaritan. The Clerk may take comfort from hearing the

pay far services not rendered jingling in It is pockets while the afflicted are made comfortless by pttying what, perhaps, they absolutely require for the decencies if not the necessaries of lite. Clergymen are wont, to expect spiritual benefit from afflictions. They go to mourners with the hope that they shall find tliein softened, subdued and changed by their sad experience. They are anxious to remove every source of irritation þÿ every thing which may divert the thoughts of the sufferers from the right use of their visitation. But at the very threshold of their efforts they are met with an obstacle. An outraged sense of justice clamors for a hearing and, in many cases, not only interferes with but actually takes the place of the salutary influences graciously assigned to the death of a relative Hold before a man tortured by the loss of bis wife or his child a large bill for services not tendered and you inevitably divert his mind from the sanctifying effect with which God has endowed all distress, to thoughts of t ho rapacity of the law or the individual who makes the calamity an occasion for a grievous and unearned charge You excite anger whore your duty is to promote composure aud reflection ; and you turn into the current of animosity what else might have co-operated with consoling and converting grace. The charge is obnoxious becr.use it is a tax on the dead for the benefit of an individual. While a man lives his property is assessed, and in proportion to it does he pay for the support

of government. When he dies the property remains and pays the same charges, with others contingent on tlio settlement of his estate. But he cannot die without paying a pet son, perhaps an utter stranger, and one, it may he, whom ho will not recognise, -814 40 or more ! The man may he his enemy þÿ may have stood in his way in a multitude of transactions þÿ may be one whom the family would not tolerate under their roof at the funeral or at any other time þÿ still he must have his lee ! That was one of the understood conditions in the event of the death ! The life of the individual tnay have been very unprofitable to the Clerk of t'ie Lutheran Church: his death, however, compensates; for that this official must he paid. A little may be said in behalf of the enactment. It is not every body who has to pay this tax. The Moravians and the Jews are exempt. They need not pay the official unless they employ him. Let us be thankful that we have that fragment of justice. But, lot me ask, by what principle is a discrimination thus made against the English and Roman Catholic Churches? What have these portions of the community done that should require them to pay penalties when they die from which other portions arc free ? Arc they worse citizens ? Do they pay less to government and officials while they live ? Do they not pay, by very far, the largest proportion of the taxes of the

1 island ? And, by consequence, as the Lutheran Church ( Clerk included) is supported by common tax, do they not pay enough during life for that of whiclt they are not either part or parcel, to be exempt from further payment wh. ti they die? They do not complain that though their congregations and churches are much larger than that, of the Lutheran persuasion, they are compelled to pay the principal part of the salaries of the ministers and other officets of that persuasion þÿ salaries much greater than they pay their own ministers and their subordinates þÿ but they do complain that when they die they must pamper an individual they had supported while they lived and whom their estates, if they have any, must continue to support. They do complain that this individual can and will charge largely for doing nothing even at their own minister's funeral. The law is injurious because it provokes acerbity in the community. Wherever a deatlt occurs, and there is a chance of getting the fee, the claim is pressed. The sense of injustice causes every one in the eircle of the deceased to participate iu the natural indignation. It tints happens that, sooner or later, the entire island becomes affected by this feeling. Is this a result to he desired? Does it contribute to the general respect with which all law should he regarded ? If the whole island is thus made to feel that one enactment is oppressive will other enactments be likely to obtain their due observance? If the injustice of one law is so

prominent may not suspicion be throws upon others ? And, therefore, for the sake of the due respect of all laws, should not this very obnoxious one be repealed ? The effect, upon the recipient of the tax is a very great objection. He is just in the attitudo of being the person whom deatlt specially favors. Other hearts may be lacerated, whole families may he desolated by an irreparable loss, while his thoughts are turned from sympathy with them by the calculation of his gain. Thus do their tears become jewels to him and their grief his happine.-s. He is injured in his relation to the community because only the sight of him suggests the fact that he represents legal injustice and reminds theobservir that ho is not slow in exacting that injustice whenever an opportunity occurs. He is injured in his moral sense because he is constantly practising on the assumption that what is accordiug to law is equitable. He is thus led to exact all he can get; and, on the principle of his exactions, if lie could be allowed one hundred or a thousand dollars for each funeral, he would have it. On that same principle, if, in drawing a will, a lawyer should write his name instead of that of some other person for whom the property was intended, he would have it ; for, by the reading of thu document, he would have a legal claim. A production before me appositely says, " the old rule, the simple plan was, ' that they should get who had the power, and they should keep who can.' But that was the rule for only

robbers and cattle stealers.'' Shylock would have the pound of flesh because "it was covenanted in the bond." In this attempt to direct attention to an unjust enactment aud to secure the co-operation of all good citizens in every proper way, to obtain its abrogation, I will not introduce all the considerations which press upon me. Let me, however, make this simple statement. The best caricature I ever saw was a pyramid of sculls, on the apex of which was a skeleton in the uumistakeable overcoat and cocked bat of Napoleon Buonaparte. The recollection of it suggests to me that this community will be apt to think a pyramid of dead bodies surmounted by an iron chest, with a certain individual complacently seated thereupon, would represent the law in question and the profits which, under it, are acquired by one who draws his living from the people through other sources. It is to be lamented there is any statute which suggests that not only vultures fatten on the dead. Respectfully yours Richard Cox.

TUESDAY, 13TII MARCH, 1SG0. þÿ þÿ We have frequently published complaints against the very obnoxious law which allows the grave-diggers in this Island to exact fees for services not rendered. No one in this community will think otherwise than that these fees ought to be abolished. We, however, cannot exactly agree with the Rector of St. John's in so far as he directs his observations so much against the grave-digger personally, instead of tho law or enactment itself. Surely, we could not expect that that individual, even if convinced that his foes are " a tax on the dead,'' should refuse to exact and receive them, and thus condemn himself and family to starvation. We entertain not the slightest doubt that he would willingly relinquish them, provided he were compensated by the State ior the loss of the revenues of his office. The intrusion of matters relating to social civilit s in the discussion of questions of this nature, does not strengthen, but, on the contrary, inly weakens the arguments of any writer.

FRANCE AND THE POPE. The following circular has been issued by the French Minister, M. Thouvenel, to the diplomatic agents of France, in reply to the last encyclical letter of the Pope : " Sir, þÿ You have read the encyclical letter which the Pope has addressed to all Patriarchs, 15. shops, and Primates of the Catholic Church, and in which iiis Holiness, explaining, in an exclusive point of view, the origin and nature of the difficulties presented hy the existing situation of the llomagna, exhorts the pastors and the faithful of the whole world to employ zenlously all their pfforts towards the maintenance and defence of the rights of the Holy See over that province. "Not doubting that this document has attracted the serious attention of the Government of , I consider it my duty to enable you to make known how His Majesty's Government appreciates " I will not for the moment stop to notice the it. reproaches, more or less explicit, which are directed hy the encyclical letter against the lino of policy followed by the Emperor with regard to the Holy S. e in the difficult circumstances of these latter times. History in its impartiality will one day say whether the r> sponsibility of the events which have occurred tails on the Sovereign whose efforts have been constantly employed to prevent them, or on those who, refusing any concession or any reform, and confining themselves to inexplicable inaction, have allowed things to grow worse and worse, until they threaten to reach a point at which the evil

will become so great that it cannot be remedied. " What in particular has attracted the painful attention of His Majesty's Government is the forgetlulness of diplomatic usages which, in so important a matter, the Court of Rome has displayed, by transporting directly to the field of religion a question which before ill things belongs to temporal order. We see with sentiments of sincere and profound regret the Holy Father appealing to the consciences of the clergy, and exciting the ardour of the faithful, with respect to an affair the discussion of which can only take place advantageously between Government and Government. ,l It is not intended, in fact, to make tho slightest encroachment on the spiritual power ol the Sovereign Pontiff, nor on the independence required for the exercise of that power within the limits of his rights. The question of the Romagua, now, as at other periods, has arisen from political circumstances ; and it is in its political aspect that we should examine it, by seeking the best means of satisfying necessities in the presence of which tho Pontifical Government would not find itself fatally placed, if,

IN Ot IR 0) n K «\ v? DR. instead of imprudently waiting for tho development of the situation, it had listened to our counsels and seconded our efforts. No, whatever a party which does not fear to assume the appearance of religious zeal may say, þÿ no, whatever may he done to lead to the belief that the interests of the faith are in peril, the question in discussion between the Government of His Holiness and that of tho Emperor is, thank God! a purely temporal one. We may therefore discuss it without failing in the deference and respect which all France feels honoured in entertaining for the Father of the Faithful, and of which His Majesty has always been happy to be the first to give the example. " I do not hesitate to say, Sir, that the Court of Rome has not been well inspired in endeavouring to establish, as the encyclical letter attempts to do, a sort of indissoluble connexion between two sorts of interests which caunot be mixed up and confounded without danger. In the first ages of the Church, when the tendencies of civilization were merely theocratical, that confusion was possible and natural ; it was accepted without difficulty by everybody, because it was in accord with the state of opinion and of men's consciences. It was thus at the outset one of the elements of the power of the Papacy, and it co-operated in the formation and development of its territorial sovereignty. Still, if we examine history with attention, we shall see clearly that it was not solely by invoking motives derived from its Di-

vine mission, and by putting forth, as it were, claims in the name of Heaven, that the Papacy, sometimes with the support of the populations themselves, sometimes with the help of foreign Sovereigns, succeed, d in gaining possession of a part of Italy. It would be seen at the same time, and tie- lact. must lie proclaimed to the holt ur of the Holy See, that the Popes found in their wisdom, their enlightenment, their love þÿ of order und ju-tice þÿ in a word, in the better government which they offered to the people in those times of violeuce and anarchy, oue of the essential clenientsof their political authority. "I will not dwell longer on this poiut of view, from the tear that, were I to do so, I should lead to the belief that. 1 atn desirous of seeking in the contrast an allusion, and of borrowing from the past a lesson applicable to the | resent times; whereas nothing is further from my thoughts. Rut I may be permitted to say that in our days, in consequence of a progress which the Emperor's Government cannot consider otherwise than as a benefit irrevocably acquired by modern societies, a separation þÿ fected between the two domains the religious bas been eforder and the civil and political one. The Holy See lias therefore placed itself in disaccord not less with the general spirit of the times than with inter-national rules, hy making an appeal to men's consciences iu the name of faith for an interest which, when rightly considered, is simply temporal. "I add that this attempt is far from being

supported by the authority and the precedents of history. In fact, this is not the first time that, at periods not far distant from our own, the situation of the Romagua and the possession of that district have been the subject of political di-cuHsion. In 1797 the Pope, in consequence of events of which he was obliged, as Sovereign, to accept the responsibility, ceded hy the treaty of Tolentino that province to France, and at the same time abandoned the ancient rights of the Holy See to the territory of Avignon ; and, great as was the regret he felt, at a diminution ol his domains, Pius VI. no doubt believed that be might subscribe to that convention without failing in his duties as Sovereign Pontiff and as guardian of the faith. The two contracting parties were not the only ones who saw in this transaction only a temporal act, in nowise encroaching on religion. The preliminaries signed at Leoben two months later between France and Austria prove that the Court of Vienna did not think differently from France on the subject. After having maintained during the war close relations with the Court of Rome Austria nevertheless supported an arrangement which awarded to her part of the States of Venetia, and indemnified the latter by transferring to them the possession of the three Legations of Romagna, Ferrara, and Bologna. The treaties of Campo Formio and Luneviile confirmed, in another form, the separation of those provinces ; and, in tho different arrangements which were then entered into it is never seen that the Go-

vernments which took part in them had to pay any attention to the prerogatives of the Holy See, as regards its spiritual power and religious interests. ' If we were to examine contemporary history on other points, who would not remember that at the beginning of this century ecclesiastical territories, such as the Bishopric of Salzburg, the Provostship of Berchtelsgaden, and the Bishoprics of Trent, B-ixen, and Eichstadt, served on the demand of Austria to indemnify its Archdukes dispossessed iu Italy ! With regard to these territories, as for tho Legations and for the Electorate of Mentz, no solidarity was recognized between the temporal rights of the possessor and the interests of religion ; the ecolesiastical character of the Sovereigns was not au obstacle to the combinations which circumstances had rendered necessary. The participation of the Court of Vienna in these different transactions certainly does not permit regarding them as an application of new principles lor the use of France. Nothing can be a better proof of this than what occurred somo years later. Pope Pius VII. was returning to Rome, and resuming the exercise of his temporal power, when, by a secret treaty signed at Naples on the 11th of January, 1814, the Emperor Francis, with a view to attaching King Joachim to the cause of the European coalition, engaged, ' in order to procure him a strong military frontier iu accord with the political necessities of the two Powers, to assure to him an

addition to the extent of 400,000 souls, to bo taken from the Roman States, and toj lend his good offices to obtain the consent andsanctiOn of the Holy Father to that concession.' ' Thus, therefore, the principle of partitioning the Legations and even the Marches between the kingdom of Naples and Austria was plainly laid down, and its application appeared so independent of every other circumstance that in the following year we see the King of the Two Sicilies, when restored to the Neapolitan throne, endeavouring to maintain for his own advantage the clause which we have just cited. Austria, on her side, was more successful in her pretensions, as she retained, at the expense of the Holy See, part of the Legation of Ferrara, on the left bank of the Po, a territory which had never belonged to the State of Venice. The Pope protested in vain against that arrangement, as he protested against the non-restitation of the county of Avignon and of the territory of Parma to the Holy See. His demands, which he based both on ancient rights aDd on reasons of utility to the Church, were not admitted by the Powers, and we shall not be contradicted bv the documents relating to the negotiations of 1815 if we add that the Rotnagna had then a very narrow escape from remaining separated frdin the Pontifical States. More than otic combination conceived in that sense was brought forward at the Congress of Vienna ; and it is well known that Prussia, for instance, proposed to dispose of the Legations in favour of the King

of Saxony, who would have received thetn as a compensation. It was not without difficulty that the Pope succeeded in retaining them and in making the right he invoked prevail over tho opinion, so worthy of remark, adopted by the plenipotentiaries, that the Legations were at the disposal of the allies by right of conquest. In any case, the discussion as to the Roman States was constantly maintained even by the Catholic Powers in an order of considerations exclusively temporal. " Such is, Sir, the sole argument I wish to draw from the examples I have cited, and which prove to what extent the doctrine advanced in the last encyclical letter, if it be at present in conformity with the ideas of the Court of Rome, ;s in contradiction to the most positive data of politics. I have no intention to draw from it arguments against the acknowledged rights of the Holy See ; but I have felt bound to furnish you with the means of rectifying around you the erroneous impressions which might tend to represent an opinion expressed on a temporal question as au attack on tho imprescriptible and sacred prerogatives of the Catholic Church. Accept, Sir, &c. " THOUVENEL."

vv ( From the New York Times, Feb. 18.) PROSPECTS OF THE TREATY AT WASHINGTON. Special Dispatch to the New York Times. Washington, Saturday, Feb. 11, 1860. There are some slight developments relative to the Mexican treaty, hut not sufficient to enable any one to judge of what its late may he. The Committee in whose hand it rests, took it up for discussion last Tuesday. Messrs. Seward, Sumner and Crittenden, it is said, declined to express any opinioD, and the Chairman not wishing to report it hack to the Senate under such circumstances, it was agreed that the matter should bo again taken up on Tuesday next, when a full expression of opinion will be given. If the Chambers of Commerce of New York and Boston understood the merits of this treaty they would instantly take action in the matter, and give their respective Senators such a suggestive poke in the ribs as would at once convince them of the propriety of going in strong for this treaty. The Southern Senators, it is understood, are ready to ratify the treaty ; hut, say they, "the direct and great benefit is to ensure to the North ; and if they are so stupid as not to see it, we shall not trouble ourselves greatly to open their eyes." This is the condition of the affair at present. The South is not euthusiastie þÿ the North is faint-hearted, suspicious and superstitious. and If the the merits ol the treaty are suppressed, negotiation is brought to naught by this unfortunate condi- tion of Northern sentiment, the remark, we " have no foreign policy, " would look very well,

cut in marble letters, over the door of the Capitol. Mr. McLane arrived on Thursday evening, but he has been too ill to attend to any kind of business. There is a considerable accumulation of advices here from Mexico. The gist ot those advices is that the reign of terror prevails in the City of Mexico and that neighbourhood, though, so far as any new expeditions against the Liberals by the Miramon faction are concerned, matters are at a stand until the fate of the treaty is known. All foreigners of property, as well as Mexicans not in league with the Church, are awaiting th eissue with intense anxiety. II the treaty is ratified by the United States Senate, Miramon will make good his escape out ot the country, and follow up the several hundred thousand dollars he is known to have sent to Europe, and the Government of Juarez will be in peaceful possession of the capital of the Republic within If sixty the days from is not ratification. treaty the date of the ratified, the civil war will be renewed more fiercely than ever, and God only knows when it will end, or bow we shall escape being involved sooner or later. This is no idle writing. Your correspondent has seen the advices, which are direct from the highest sources. The difficulties in the Juarez Cabinet have been adjusted satisfactorily to all parties. Mr. Ocampo resigned as Minister for Foreign Affairs, and was appointed to come to this country with special powers, and having completed bis mission here, he will proceed to England.

Degollado leaves the army in charge of Gen Uraga, and assumes the duties of Minister ot Foreign Affairs. The latest advices from Vera Cruz, which state that Caravajal is about to attach T mpico, are entirely a mistake. Caravajal is a Liberal chieftain, and commands one part of Uraga's troops, who are now harrasing the Church forces somewhere in the neighbourhood of Pueblo. There is reliable information from Vera Cruz that Gen. Degollado has been appointed Secretary for Foreign Affairs, to serve during the absence of Mr. Ocampo, who is expected to arrive here in the course of this week, on a special mission from the Constitutional Government, and more especially to arrange such details of the McLane treaty as are left to the Executive authorities of both Governments, including the designation of the places through which merchandise from the United States may either pass free, or at such rates of duty as our own Congress may impose. AUSTRIA. (From tho Times' Correspondent.) Vienna, Feb. 1 1. It is generally stated that this Government has rejected the prop itious made by the British Cabinet, hut such is not yet the case. It is morally certain that the fourth proposition will not be accepted by Austria, but it is not likely that she will plainly and positively deny the right of the inhabitants of Central Italy to place themselves under the must Victor Emmanuel, as she sceptre of King foresee that a violent effort will be made to reject her from Venice, if she should attempt to make a diversion in favour of the Imperial and Royal exiles. Austria is now doing all in her power to conciliate Russia, and it has been hinted to mo that she is willing to make great sacrifices if the St. Petersburg Cabinet will conclude a treaty of alliance with her. Count Frederick Thun, the Austrian Minister at St. Petersburg, is a persona, grata with the Emperor Alexander, and also with Prince Gortschakuff, but his endeavours to bring about an offensive and

ss ? . e IB ® n « vn defensive alliance between the two empires are not likely to be attended with success, as Russia is at present totally unable to wage war. The question respecting the emancipation of the serfs is still pending, and recently the tillers of the soil have become extremely refractory- The finances of Russia are in a deplorable state, anil the circumstances connected with the liquidation of tho house ofStieglitz have made the fact known to the whole world. A few days since there was a secret diplomatic gathering at Manheim, was the matter discussed and it is believed that the possibility of a renewal of the war in Italy. It is said that the parties concerned were the representatives of Austiia and of those States which met in conference at Wurzburg a few months ago. The Prussian Government, wishing to have reliable information concerning the strength and condition of the various armies in Lombard)', Tuscany, and the Romagna, has despatched General von Wildenbruck, who was formerly Minister at Constantinople, to the Italian Peninsula. As Marshal Varllant has received orders to move his troops injbrigadts towards Brescia, the Lombards trow speak of little but the approaching attack on Venetia. According to the Italians, the Austrians are to be driven back to the Isonzo, and the Pope is to be deprived of the whole of liis dominions north of the Apennines. The Austrian Government, being well aware that mischief is meant, is making preparations for giving a warm reception to its assailants. The truops

stationed in the Southern Tyrol are about to march into Venetia, and several regiments arc to be sent from this city to the south. The fortifications on the Dalmatian and Istrian coasts uro completed, but they are said to be ntuclt less efficient than they might be made. The fortresses of Verona, Legnago, Mantua, and Peschrera have received large supplies of provisions and ammunition. south-west poiuts to be fortified on the The principal frontier of the empire (the Southern Tyrol) are the so-called Wurmser Joch, the Tonal Pass, and the Monte Buldo, near Corona and Spiazze. For the moment simple blockhouses are likely to be constructed. Barons vou Vay and Pronay left for l'esth last night, and it is to be leareit that they failed to come to an understanding with the Government. The Minister for Ecclesiastical Affairs has carried his point, as his ordinances will be maintained, but he would have rendered his Sovereign and country better service if he had allowed the members of the, Synods to be chosen by the Seniorats instead of the superintendeuctes. How many ugly rubs might not Austria have escaped during the last year if Iter rulers bad been less dogmatical ! The Austrian Government is so accustomed to command at home, that it every now aud then attempts to do the same thing abioad, aud is surpiised aud hurt if it gets snubbed for its pains. As Idolatry has long been in fashion here, it is but natural that the Emperor should consider himself a much greater personage than any other living

being. It strikes me, that, if His Majesty it would visit oilier countries tor a short time, would be of equal advantage to lrimsell and his subjects. TRIAL OF MR. WIIITWORTIT S RI- FLED CANNON. The first experimental trials of tho ranges and accuracy of Mr. YVliitworth's breeeh-loailing cannon, having the peculiar hexagonal bore and firing the long six-sided cone, which form the basis of that gentleman's principle of rifled ordnance, were made here during yesterday and to-day. The results, which have been so long looked forward to with eagerness by Artillerymen and Engineers, surpassed the most sanguine expectations. The success, in fact, was really astounding. The accuracy of fire and length of range obtained from trifling charges of powder were so totally beyond what lias ever yet been attained that it is evident we are upon the eve of another revolution in all relating to scientific gunnery, and that even the greatest results which have ever been obtained from the Aimstrong gun are likely to be in turn surpassed by Mr. Whitworth's ordnance. It is a very general though not the less an erroneous opinion to suppose that each great improvement is to be the last of its kind, and thus with the manufacture of Armstrong's admirable cannon, possessing such qualities of range, accuracy, and penetration as to be removed from any degree of comparison with the old ordnance, it was thought that the ne plus ultra ot gunnery had been attained, and that further improvement was hopeless. The truth is, however, that in beginuing with a rifled breech-loader we have merely made the lead path, which may first step in an entirely new to effective results even yet considered beyond attainment. It is only

within tho last two or three years that scientific men have at all directed their attention to the laws which govern the flight of all projectiles, and have studied the mechanical condition which these require iu the form of shot anil rifling of gun The Armstrong gun was a gigantic stride in the progress of scientific gunnery, but the experiments which have just been made at this place show that it is not the last we must expect, and that, though at present greater than all others in range and precision, even the Whitworth gun in both these points may be surpassed by others before the year is out. As the guns are all alike iu every respect but proportions of size, a description of one will suffice. The piece may, in familiar terms, bo said to consist of a tube rifled throughout from muzzle to brcecli ; the breech is closed, when the gun Is loaded, by a cap, ir shape something like the cap of a telescope. The cap is fitted on the breech end of the tube, which is screwed externally to receive it. It is never wholly removed like the breech-piece of an Armstrong, btit turns and works in an iron hoop, which is connected with a projection at the side of the breech by a hinge joint, on which it swivels sideways. One great advantage of this plan of construction is that it enables the whole length of the barrel to be rifled, and thus eyery inch of it becomes effective as a gun, which is not i the case when a chamber or other breech-loading apparatus, as in Armstrong's for instance,

occupies the breech of the piece. At the first glance it is difficult to realize the fact that the 3-pounder þÿ the long, thin tube, like a telescope on wheels, and only weighing 2081b. þÿ can really be one. of the most formidable engines which the science of modern warfare has produced, þÿ a terrible weapon, capable, with a charge of powder not very much greater than is used in a large duck gun, of dealing almost certain death at. a distance of five miles. As compared with tho bluff', thick, flat muzzled service gun of a year ago, both Armstrong's and Whitworth's guns seem almost to be animated by an instinct or intelligence of their own ; and nothing would more forcibly illustrate the triumph of mind over matter than to see the cumbrous mass of iron now called a 68-pounder placed side by side with Whit worth 3-pounder tube, capable of destroying its pon- derous antagonist at a distance of 10,000 yards ' þÿ English Paper.

THE SCIENCE OF THE WEATIIEH. In these restless inquisitive times, when the discovuiH s u i s acute ure multiplying so rapidly tliat simple folks ure almost beginning to tear everything will soon be found out, and that the Humboldts and Faradays of coming generations will have to sit down and cry, as Alexander did of old, because nature has no more mysteries for them to unravel, it does seem strange that the very class of phenomena we take most interest in, and have the best opportunities of observing, should have been, until a very few years back, little better than a sealed book to us, and should be even now the one we are most ignorant of. Yet so it is Of all subjects, the weather is the one about which there is the most universal interest, as well as we might almost say, the most universal ignorance. We are always thinking and talking about it þÿ and no wonder, since our harvests, our commerce, our amusements and social life, our health and mortality, are all directly controlled by its changes. There arc more proverbs about the weather than about anything else; and in our owu and several other countries, a meteorological wish is the first greeting among friends, ana a meteorological observation the starting-point of conversation amoDg strangers. We are most of us instinctive barometers. As Hudibras says : Old sinners have all points O' th' compass iu their bones and joints, Can by their pangs and aches find All turns and changes ot the wind. And yet, though there is nothing wo are more

eager to find out all about, we have only set to work to investigate the subject systematically within the last twenty or thirty years, and are now barely across the threshold of the science, and still woefully in the dark. The great fault of the old school of meteorologists was their haste to begiu reading the future before they had mastered the past, and their blind reliance on their own isolated and imperfect experience. After a few years' apprenticeship as observers, they generally started in business as prophets, with a limited capital of very doubtful facts to work upon ; and ended either by becoming confirmed quacks, or retiring in disgust at the failure of their predictions. Gradually, however, the conviction dawned on the minds of those who paid attention to the matter, that tbey had begun by attempting too much, and that, after all, the apparent irregularity and caprice of the weather was due only to their own limited vision ; so they became more humble in their views, put the prophet's robes 011 the shelf in the meantime, and resolved to begin at the beginning, in the hope that, by observing the fluctuations of the weather more clorely and systematically, and over a wider area, they might find some method in its maduess. Not without much nudging and memorialising, our own and various foreign governments were induced to give their aid to the enterprise ; and about twenty years ago, general system a of meteorological observations was organised over a great part of the

civilised world. The official impulse given to the study of this important science, euli fed many able and industrious volunteers iu the work, and there are now thousands of keen eyes, all the world over, on land and sea, busy watching and recording the vagaries of the weather þÿ which way the wind blows, and what sort of temper it is in, the amount of rain-fall, the moisture of the air, the height of the temperature, and so on. The new mode of studying j the weather has been attended, so far as it has gone, with the most encouraging success. Wo have not advanced very far as yet, but at least we are not without a sign that we are on the right track at last, and every day wo are advancing our lamp further into the obscurity which has so long enveloped the subject. Although no fixed and definite method has been discovered in the variations of the weather, enough has been accomplished to enable us to have a short but very useful warning of any great atmospheric changes. A general law, for instance, has been traced, by moans of the barometer, in the undulation of that shoreless, aerial ocean whose mighty waves roll unceasingly over our heads, and on the bed of which we walk about. As the crest or the trough of a wave passes on high, the glass rises or falls ; and in the curve formed by these oscillations of the barometer, may be seen an exaot miniature of

Si If, MOI. X the wave above. In certain cases, the same curve has been observed during the same period of successive years; and lieuce itis inferred thatsuch waves are periodical in their appearance. One enormous wave pays 1 = a visit once a year, in the mouth of Govern 1, arc rding to Mr. Birt, occupies foui in its transit, and moves along at the ineteen miles an hour, so that its whole i.st, he not less than 6000 miles ! This ic wave is the one which did so much dainag. to the allied fleets in the Black Sea during the Crimean war. It began to play havoc with the ships at Balaklava just four days after it left London, so that had meteorology been more popular, by the aid ot the electric telegraph and barometric observations, the allied navies might have had timely warning of the unwelcome visitor, and sought shelter from its fury. Then, again, the two gales which wrecked so many vessels in November last were distinctly foretold, accordiug to Admiral Fiizroy of the Meteorological Department of the Admirality. On both occasions, the barometer was very low ; but before the advent of the first gale, the thermometer was low, and high before that of the second. It was, therefore, interred that there would bo two gales, aud that the first would come from the north, while the other would come from the south, which turued out to be the case. Indeed, it has now been ascertained that no gale of any consequence comes upon us without due ' note of preparation' being given by the barometer. The longer the duration of the

storm, the longer is the waruing of its approach, as it to give more time to prepare for it, while a sudden notice is uever followed by more tbau a brief gale. I11 this way the thermometer indicates the quarter from which that storm is coming, which the barometer tells u- is a hand ; and the aspect of the ky, and the record ot the past weather, help us to eke out the information thus derived. By carefully collating the observations of the direction aud intensity of the wind contained in the log-books of upwards of ten thousand vessels, Lieutenant Maury has succeeded iu drawing out a complete chart of the various currents of the atmosphere in every part of the world at all times ol the year. Ot course, the currents indicated in these maps are subject to occasional aberrations from various causes ; hut they exhibit, at least, very clearly aud definitely, the course of the main atmospheric tides. At a glance, the captain of a ve-sel can see whether ho will have any very troublesome .vitids to deal with iu the part of the ocean he is about to traverse at any particular time of the year, and can shape his course so as to avail himself of favourable winds, aud steer clear of such as would impede his voyage or eudaugcr his vessel. By this means voyages to some parts of the world have already been shortened by a third, and even in a few cases by half of five usual time, while the risk and expense have been greatly reduced. With the course of the wiuds, both rain and temperature are intimately eouueeted. The ex-

tremes of our weather depend on the UDcqual prevalence ot one or other of the two great currents of air, the polar and the equinoctial, whose ceaseless rivalry keeps the atmosphere in a state of wholesome agitation. The former, cold and dry, sends the barometer up, and the thermometer down ; while the other, warm aud moist, has just the opposite effect. Compensation appears to be the great law of temperature, excess in one direction being atoned for by excess in another. The average temperature of a place, it has been found, remains nearly the same, an unusually hot summer being generally followed by an unusually cold winter, aud the wider the area we take into consideration, the more 1 H is the equilibrium maintained In this wu a tuild European winter is made up of a ver 1 e one in Asia or America, or vice versa From the fate of the other side of the world, we may therefore gain some idea of what wo have to expect lor ourselves. The causes on which the fall of rain depends arc still in dispute among meteorologists ; some contending that air is capacitated to take up and hold water by its high temperature alone, and that the return of the water in the form of rain is duo to tho lowering of temperature ; while others insist that the process is not complete without the agency of electricity. A few years

ago, a gentleman, adopting tho view that the drops of rain are kept aloft in the heavens by means of electricity, and that every spark ol electricity drawn away will release so much water, published a little work with the somewhat startling title, How to Produce Ruin at Will , in which he proposed to bring down a shower whenever it was wanted by means of kites with iron frames, or some other conductor equally light, to soar to the clouds; and there seems little doubt the thing can be done, though not to any useful extent, from the difficulty of getting any conductor near the clouds large enough to attract more than a very small quantity of electricity, and consequently to release more thau a very small drizzle of rain. The tendency of thickly wooded districts to be very rainy would seem to support the electricity j and theory Green trees are capital conductors, high enough to bring down electricity under certain circumstances ; and it is a notorious fact, that a general destruction of forests frequently leads to excessive droughts, and sometimes even destroys the fertility of a district. The general opinion appears to be, that both temperature and electricity have to do with rain, though it may ho doubted which is the cause and which the consequence of its fall. As an illustration of precipitation from the mixture of warm with cold and moist air, the curious fact is put forward, that on the occasion of a crowded hall in Sweden, when the heat was so great that a ladv fainted, a window was broken to admit a ,

immediately it snowed in the room. The Btudy of such records of the w.-atli s we have already obtained has tended to »t:( en the belief, previously entertained among tno-e most deeply versed in the science, that tlTe weather is governed by a definite system of periodical rotation. What its cycle may be, we can, as yet, do no more than guess at; but many competent authorities cherish the hope, that the time will cotne when meteorologists rnav conscientiously add the office of prophet to that of historian, and predict the changes of the weather as surely and precisely as we now do the fluctuations of the ocean and the process of the suns. ' Had ' made Hipparchus hourly observations, and had they been and Ptolemy,' says one writer, tnade also by their contemporaries and successors in different parts of the world, wc might now have been predicting the weather with as much certainty as we do the planetary motions.' According to Mr. Glaisher, there is a rotation in the character of the weather every fifteen years þÿ the seasons growing warmer and warmer till they reach their warmest point ; and then gradually colder, till they get to the coldest point, when they begin the round of temperature again. If this theory be correct, a new cycle commenced in 1853, when, the maximum of cold having been reached, warmth began to predominate over cold, and will continue to ascend till 1861, when cold will once more mount the ladder. Mr. Luke Howard gives ten years as the cycle of fluctuation ; and vari-

ous other weatherwiso folk have their pet theories. It would be premature as yet to lay much stress on such calculations ; but it is certainly a very suggestive fact, that the price of wheat þÿ which of course is influenced by the weather þÿ lias exhibited in this country a regular and invariable oscillation of four years up and four years dowu, for the last thirty-two years. To many, no doubt, the weather-tables of Mr. Glaisher and others innst appear very dull and uninteresting indeed ; and yet it requires no magic spectacles to read in them the ' story of our lives from year to year ;' rich harvests and expanding commerce, good health, plenty, and contentment ; or perhaps the gloomier side of the picture þÿ scanty crops and high prices, stagnant trade and social irritation, prevalent disease and busy death. But deeper still is the interest they derive from the prospect that, in the course of time, they will not only reflect for us tho past, but may even forecast the future, and enable us, by timely foreshadowing of the coming weather, to avail ourselves of its bounties, while we guard against its þÿravages. S 1\ 0 B 0 I. A V I. COMMUNICATION. A TAX OA THE IHIAJ. To the Editor of the St Croix Avis, Dear sir, The letter which appeared in ilie Avis of the 13tli instant, over the signature ot the Revd. Mr. Cox, in reference to the injustice of the law þÿ oft, and universally complained of þÿ which entitles the Clerk of the Lutheran Chuich to claim certain specified fees, with regard to funerals, for services neither rendered nor required of him, has, it would appear, beeu designedly misrepresented, and made the occasion of many unfair remarks ; his ohvious inteut and meaning has þÿ for no kind purpose, the public may he sure þÿ beet) wilfully perverted, and a coloring attempted to he given to some of his expressions neither meant nor implied by the writer, nor which, the shallowest knowledge of the real meaning of language can bear them out iu even supposing. Mr. Cox's letter is before the public, and therefore open to fair and unbiased criticism He has stated his views through the proper and legitimate channel þÿ through which all uured. ssed public grievances or oppressions should be made known and discussed ; and the same medium is open to others to represent their views who may dissent from anything which the Revd. Gentleman has stated. But I must protest against the meanness and injustice of the unmanly practice þÿ so prevalent, 1 am sorry to say, in this Island þÿ of those who, under galleries, and in stores give vent to the had feelings within, iu order to arouse prejudice, and lasli themselves into unwarrantable excitement, and the enunciation of expressions which

they would be ashamed to put upou paper. Mr. Cox may have said more than was necessary on tho occasion, hut a great deal more has been made of what he did say than is generous or warranted. Those persons must he considered enemies to Government, and to society, who are ever ready þÿ and the (act is to be regretted þÿ to produce division between different classes of a community by attributing false motives, drawing false conclusions, and by endeavouring to give a certain bias to every incident which may arise to offer them an opportunity of gratifying their disposition in this respect. That alt open mouthed cry of alarm should arise from officials, may not, perhaps, he so much wondered at, þÿwhenever what they choose to regard as vested rights þÿ are touched upon in any instance, let the fees or emoluments upon which these, so called, rights are founded be ever so grievous or oppres-ive to any portion of the community. But, it is to be hoped they will become more accustomed to these thiugs as time advances, and the march of liberal sentiment evolves a prop r knowledge of those principles by which men have a right to freely animadvert upon, and express their opinions regarding an unjust or obnoxious law, without being liable to be charged with a hostile or personal offence against the individual who may happen to be the executive recipient under the law at the time. I am, Dear sir, your ob. serv Justice.

Another act has been played out in the great Drama of Italian Affairs. The Emperor Napoleon has forwarded propositions to Turin for the settlement of the Italian Question These propositions arc the abandonment of the annexation of Tuscany to Piedmont, the Tuscan people being allowed to select their own Sovereign, with tho exception of Prince Napoleon and the Prince of Carigan. The Duchies of Parma and Modcna are to be annexed to Piedmont, and Victor Emmanuel will also administer the Romagna, under the suzcrainetk of the Pope, if the Pope accept it, and, if not.

without it. These propositions were accompanied with a menace that in case the Piedmontese Government did not accept, this arrangement, the French army was to be recalled from Lombardy. To these propositions it is announced that M Cavour's acceptance is known, but with the addition tlia' the various populations shall be consulted by means of universal suffrage. The opening of the French legislative Session of 1860 took place on the 1st inst The speech of the Emperor, was expected with more than ordinary interest Being too lengthy for this paper, we are Constrained to extract it in part. His Majesty spoke as follows: þÿ '' Messieurs les Senateurs, " Messieurs les Deputes, "On the opening of last session, relying upon the patriotism of France, 1 endeavoured to fortify your minds in advance againsi the exaggerated apprehensions of a probable war. To-day I have at heart to reassure you against the anxiety cans d by peace itself. That peace I desire sincerely, and shall neglect nothing to maintain it. ''The dominant idea of the Treaty of Villa franca was to obtain the ;,lm >st complete, independence ofVeuetia at the price of the est oration ot the Archduk s. That tr, nsaction having failed, despite my most earnest endeavours, 1 have expressed my regret thereat at Vienna as well as at Turin, for the situation by being prolonged threatened to lead to no issue. While it was the object of frank explanations between my Government and that of Austria, it suggested to England, to Prussia,

to llu-sia, measures th whole ot which clearly prove on the part of the Great Powers their desire to obtain a reconciliation of all the interests. " To second these dispositions it was necessary for France to present that combination the adoption of which would have the greatest chance of being accepted by Europe. Guaranteeing Italy by my army against foreign intervention, I had the right to assign the limits of that guarantee Therefore I did not, hesitate to declare to the King of Sardinia that, while having liim lull liberty ol action, I could not follow him in a policy which had the fault of appearing in the eyes of Europe a desire to absorb all the States of'Italy, and which threatened new conflagrations I counselled him to reply favourably to the wishes of the provinces which should offer themselves to him, hut to maintain the, independence of Tuscany, and to respect in principle the rights of the Holy See. If this arrangement does not satisfy everybody, it has the advantage of reserving principles, of calming apprehensions, and makes Piedmont a kingdom of more than 9,000,000 souls. " Looking to this transformation of Northern Italy, which gives to a powerful State all the passes of the Alps, it was my duty, for the security of our frontiers, to claim the French slopes of the mountains. This rea-sertion of a claim to a territory of small extent has nothing iu it of a nature to alarm Europe and give a denial to the policy of disinterestedness which I have proclaimed more than once, for France

does not wish to proceed to this aggrandizement, however small it may be, either by military occupation or by provoked insurrection, or by underhand manoeuvres, but by frankly explaining the question to the Great Powers. They will doubtless understand in their equity, as France would certainly understand it for each of them under similar circumstances, that the important territorial arrangement which is about to take place gives us a light to a guarantee indicated by nature herself. " The protectiou of Providence, so manifestly on our side during the war, will not tail to a peaceful enterprise whose object is the improvement of the lot of the greatest number Let us continue, then, firmly our path to progress, without allowing ourselves to be arrested either by the menaces of selfishness, or by the clamours of parties, or by unjust suspicions. THE AUSTRIAN REPLY TO THE EN- GUSH PROPOSITION. The following has been received at Mr. Ueuter's office : þÿ Vienna, Friday. The answer of the Austrian Cabinet to the English proposal, to M. Thouvenel, remitted prince Metternicb which has been bears date by the 17th February. The message of Count de Rechherg commences by expressing the nigh estimation attached by the Government of his Apostolic Majesty to the communication from Franco. The Austrian Minister is happy to discover in these friendly steps an ardent desire to maintain a cordial understanding between the two Courts. Pnssing to the examination of the four points proposed by England, Count de Rochberg points out. under the question of intervention, two essential things þÿ: 1st. The principle of the right of intervention ; and þÿ 2nd. The opportunity for its application. Without prejudging the principle in any way, the Austrian Cabinet recognises that, in the present circumstances' there is no opportunity either for Austria or France to interfere in Central Italy. The second point, ns Count Rechberg observes, now drawn her troops from all parts of Italy applies to Franoe alone, Austria having not with- under her domination. Referring to the third point, which regards the interior organisation of Venctia, Count Rechberg declares that, although this question muBt remain quite extraneous to the negotiations between the Powers, the Emperor of Austria loyally maintains all the promises of Villafranca as regards Venctia. If

these promises have not yet been realised, the fault can only be attributed to the intrigues and continual provocations of the Italian revolutionary party, which no longer conceals its intention of turning these concessions against Austria herself, in order deprive to her of Venctia. As regards the fourth point, Count Recbbcrg considers it useless at the present moment to engage in a discussion of the principle of the proposed combination the settlement of tho for affairs of Italy. Austria confines herself to the expression of her own conviction that the re-establishment of the former dynasties, and the realisation of the project of an Italian confederacy, would much better guarantee the future of the Peninsula. She will leave it to time and the course of events to confirm the justice of hor judgment.

Monday the 31st Oct. 1859 the Burgher Council Held a session extra ordinem when the following matters were referred : The subject concerning the reduction of taxes was taken into consideration, and haviug discussed the several items in connection with the same, the Council agreed in the following points : On piinciple the revenues of the Commune ought not to be calculated to more than what is required to cover the expenditure, and the the late unfavorable years, to pay notwithstanding Land Treasury bad been able, off a considerable debt; there might thciefore be question of effecting a reduetion of the Land Treasury taxes approximating to the average surplus of $6000 to $7000 ; yet on account of the somewhat precarious and varying nature of s me of the sources of revenue, particularly of the Absentee-tax, and the probability of increased expense in several communal branches, it was not considered advisablo to fix the reduction now contemplated at more than $5000. I he Cavalry and Artillery tax has been acknowledged by all parties as that which first and principally ought to he considered ; giving an auaual revenue ol $6889 apportioned on all the sugar estates without any regard to tlreir present value or productiveness, it is very oppressive on the smaller and less productive estates, which are otherwise unfavorably placed, especially as regards the direct tax on cane land, 1 he taxes on the properti s in the towns also

require consideration on account of their present circumstances and the low value of houses and rents. These taxes þÿ the House-tax, 4 per cent on the annual value or rent, and New-tax \ Cent pr. square ell of the measurement þÿ amount to about $6041, and are not sufficient to defray the communal expenses for one branch for the towns population, say the Poor Department. 1 tie New-tax is acknowledged as that least of all apportioned to the value and revenue of the properties, but the unfairness of this latter mode ol taxation would bo alleviated in a very trifling degree il the Land Treasury discontinued it, because the State Treasury levies the same (the Building tax) with 3 times the amount. It was therefore agreed upon, to reduce the House-tax, 4 per cent, to the half or 2 per cent on the rents, whereby the present revenue about $3400 would be reduced to about $1700. This reduction in addition to the discontinuance of the Cavalry and Artillery tax, $6880, would however cause a diminution of $8580 of the revenue, thus exceeding the amount which according to the above is proposed to bo reduced ($5000), with $3580. A minority of members however proposed, that for the present the reduction should be limited to half the Cavalry and Artillery-tax, say $3440, which amount in addition to the reduction of half the House-tax, say $1700, would give $5140, thus making up the amount mentioned above, for this reason, that the existing relations do not admit of the introduction of

any new impost, which would be required, if the whole amount of the Cavalry and Artillery-tax should be done away with ; moreover that an increase of others of the revenues would enable the Laud Treasury within a short time to discontinue the remaining half of this tax so oppressive and inequitably apportioned. The majority maintained, that the opportunity be taken at once to do away with the Artillery and Cavalry-tax, and proposed that the deficiency of $3580 be covered by a new impost affecting the same interest, the sugar-production, but levied iu a fairer proportion to the productivity of the estates. hor obtaining this there was suggested an import-duty on all the articles duty-free according to the ordinance of 30th June 1850 6 I. a, with the exception offish, vegetables, books and furniture þÿ calculated at a permanent duty (4 a 5 per Cent, advalorem ), calculated to give an annual revenue of $3500, even excepting such articles when imported from Denmark. The accounts of the Customs for the years 1854 to 1859 show an annual average value of about $90,000 of the articles in question imported tree of duty during that period. To this proposal it was objected, partly that it. is matter of doubt, if the amount calculated would be obtainable, partly that pome of the articles, such as coals and mules ought to continue duty-free; the calculation of duty on machinery &c. would also be connected with difficulties. It was ultimately agreed, to address the Government on the subject and propose, that the

amount in question be raised in the following manner : 1. By impost-duty on staves and heading, calculated at 450 M. p. a $3 p. M. $1,350. þÿ þÿ wood hoops 250 M. a $4 p M. 1,000. þÿ iron hoops, about 50,000 lb. at empty puncheons, 550 a 10 Ct. 55. 30 Ct. p. 100 lb 150.
2. By an increase of the New-tax on cane-land (16 Ct. pr. acre) with 5J Ct. 1,015.

From the St. Thomas Times, March 17. SANTO DOMINGO. The following information, derived from a source we have reason to place implicit reliance on, reached us by the last mail; it describes some very extraordinary scenes recently enacted at Santo Domingo: þÿ Santo Domingo, 6th March 1860. On the 24th February a very gross insult was offered to the French nation by the Government ; on that day the tricolor flag, which is everywhere regarded with great respect, was during several hours paraded in the principal streets of the city underneath a Dominican flag ; for this purpose it appears that a procession had been formed, to which an official character was given by the presence of drummers of the army under the command of a General in full uniform and it was followed by a large mob who amused themselves with committing the most gross outrages upon the French flag amid the general derision, hisses and screams of the rabble. The procession at last went to the French Consulate and in the presence of the French Consul and of the British and Spanish Consuls, who were in the balcony, repeated the insults in the most disgusting manner and with uproarious noise. M. Saiut Andre, the French Consul, supported by Mr. Hood and by Mr. Alvarez, the English and Spanish Consuls, made an energetic demand for reparation. On the 20th this was given, the French flag being on that day saluted with 21 guns and a Proclamation being published throughout the city, iu which the Government expressed its regret at the recent outrage. The greatest excitement prevailed iu the populace ,

and for some days the lives of the Consuls were, it is supposed, in imminent danger They deserve great praise for the courage and energy with which they grappled the question, obtaining immediate satisfaction for the insult offered, and preventing tiie enacting of other very revolting sceues which were publicly spoken of. This conduct ou the part o! the Sto. Domingo Government, or its creatuies, is attributed to their desire to have revenge for the salutes to the British anil French flags which they were obliged to liie io December last, previous to the landing of the Consuls, on their return to Sto. Domingo, and also for the unfavorable answers, it is saiil, that the Domiuican Government have received to a famous memorandum ou the subject ol tlioso salutes which they had addressed to the British and French Governments.
