With regard specially to the instance of auditing the accounts, this is a subject which of all appears least qualified to be left to the exclusive control of the local authorities It lias been his particular wish to obtain for the Colonies the services of a man of theoretical knowledge and experience for those objects, which the Committee lias had in view in alluding to an officer of engineers, but he must agree with the 3d member for Ftederiksted in tlie opinion that it will be imprac- | ticable for the home-Goverument to semi out ail officer, as they require all t ho talents of which they have the disposal, for their own use. A civil engineer might be lud, if there was sufficient employment and remuneration for bis services here, but this is uot likely to be tlie case even with a considerable assistance from tlie public funds. The 1st member for Fredcriksted, Sarauw, stated that, he is prevented from as-entiug to the increase iu the pay of the comptrollers, because this increase is determin, d for every 4 instead of every 5 years as is the rule in other analogous cases, and because the salary burins with $1000 instead of $900 as fixed by "the Royal Resolution of 1850. The Governor replied, that in the cases that might serve as an analogy, the rule is sometimes 3, sometimes 5 years, and that the 4th year had been chosen as the middle-course. The 3d member for Christiansted, BuBois,

remarked that generally a more favorable scale is adopted tor public officers in the colonies than in the mother country, and that in the english colonies the rate is 4 years for 6 years in Europe. The Governor stated, respecting the $300 proposed as an increase in tlie salary for the Secretary at St Thomas that the anticipation objected to in the Report of the Committee already exists in the item of $2500, and that the object aimed at in the proposal id the draft, namely to induce well qualified persons to apply for the situation will he frustrated if the higher salary is not ready to be offered whenever the vacancy occurs As for the increased salary for the Treasurer in St. Thomas it is true, that tlie total amount passing through his hands is less titan that passing through those of the Treasurer of Sr. Croix, but the items forming that amount are greater in number, and that the expense of living is higher tin re than here, besides which the sum required f r the expenses of the Office is rated too low llis Excellency disapproved of tlie i riuriple of making up for low salaries by pcsonal supplements as proposed in the pies nt case by the Committee, as experience g, u rally shows that the most deserving are the least clamorous for these kind of gratuities, as they me naturally disinclined to beg for that as a favour to which they feel themselves entitled in justice and equity. He also objected to the giant of a separate salary for a Judge Advocate for the military jurisdiction, particular in St Thomas,

where tlie functions of the Judge are not so numerous as in this island The 5th member for Christiansted, Kotin , replied to tlie observations of the Governor on the increased salary for the. Secretary in St. Thomas, that the objection alluded would be easily obviated, by allowing tlie vacancy to last somewhat longer, until the Colonial Council could be heard on the question, whether the existing circumstances would warrant the additional expense. With regard to the pay to the Treasurer in St. Thomas the Committee has been guided by the consideration that the qualifications for the due fulfilment, of the Office are any thing but rare and such as may easily be found in individuals that would consider the existing rate of salary a highly desirable object. Several of the French miliiary off duty were wounded iu the melee; a major received a Sabre cut and a heavy blow with the flat of a broadsword on his head; another offi-

cer, a nephew of the General of Division, was wounded in the left arm. The whole body of the French officers show the utmost indignation. They arc angry against the General, who, they think, did not sufficiently exert himself to prevent such an iniquitous deed. Cap tain Gorde, the man who turned French bayonets against the people at the beginning of the fray, has been challenged by 16 of his fellowofficers. He has been expelled from the club and mess (casino and pension.) A protest has been drawn up, to which all the officers have Put their signatures, and which was handed to the General by the Colonel of the 40th. The General has given out an order of the day in which he expresses his regret " at the excesses which had been perpetrated." llis words, however, are rather ambiguous, and the conduct of the Gendarmes is eulogized in the main. Ho went in the very evening of Monday, at 9, to the barracks of the Gendarmes, and there expressed his approbation of their conduct. The Gendarmes at Monte Citorio had one hour before received the thanks of Mousiguor Matteucci in the Pope's name, aud, what they valued far more, five sciidi a-head for the men aud ten for the non commissioned officers þÿ tho price of blood. keep public order in Rome at any cost, lest upon the provocation of the slightest disturbance the Pope should be induced to run away. Tomorrow the same intimation will be conveyed to the officers of the 40th. By the Royal Ordinance of May 14th 1823, it was enacted, that, in order to enable proprietors of plantations to obtain credit, which, ou account of the preferable claims of other creditors, was not easy, and in order to prevent a state of tilings, by which tho negroes on the plantations might bo exposed to want the support, which according to justice and humanity it would under all circumstances be the duty of Government to assist them in obtaining from the estates to which they belong, þÿ advances of supplies or money made for that purpose, might be secured a preferable payment from the crop they had assisted in establishing, before all other claims against the estates, and even before the taxes. The ordinance then proceeds to lay down the rules and the forms to be observed by those who would give or obtain advances and

S> CHOI ft V (| S supplies under this Act, and an administration was established, under whose control all the transactions must be effected, and whose certificates, called Burcau-Gertificates, establish a preferable right in the Crop tor the claim which they certify. This exceptional law was obviously intended to act upon, and enacted with regaid to the then existing system of Slavery and the relations contingent thereon, and from this point of view it may to a certain degree be defended. But, it was at best a serious interference with credit and with the relations between creditors and deb tors, and it legalized a violent and unheard of in'nad in the rigtits and securities of mortgageholders. As might he expected, the law was from its very beginning abused, and the facilities it created for obtaining credit, were turned iuto very different operations. Unscrupulous persons made use ot the institution as a sham, under cover of which they carried on most nefarious transactions tor tho purpose of cheating their creditors. A few of such transactions were so barefacedly impudent as to be easily found out, and a tew lawsuits arose, some of them criminal suits ; hut in infinitely many more cases, the perpetrators gained their end unpunished. Prudent and conscientious men in this Colony always have condemned the Bureauinstitution, and would have nothing to do with it ; and as it tended greatly to impair the existing mortgage-debts ou plantations, and was he-ides liable to much concealed abuse, it spee-

dily fell into Lad repute, and was lor a scries of years very sparingly usid. The institution even became so disreputable, as to affect most tin pleasantly the credit of planters who put their estates iuto the Bureau; and it is only of late years, siuee everything has retrograded in this Island, since insolvency is paraded about, and the most needy presume to be tho loading men, that the Bureau has come iuto some favor, for it is naturally an appendage to insolvency. When Slavery was abolished here, this institution ought to have ceased also, as founded mainly upoD and for the state of Slavery, in fact, for the sustenance of the Slaves. But, instead of being abolished, the Bureau-Institution was, to tho contrary, made ampler and more fully developed, and bolstered up in a multitude of ways, þÿ and of course, the poorer the country became, the gi eater ebcamc the use made of this pnns asivorum, and the greater the use the more aud the greater also the abuses. The state of tilings brought, about by this Institution, is truly deplorable ; for, coutrary to its aitn, it has annihilated credit, created distrust, and increased the diflficul'ies of Planters. Who will invest a dollar in a property, or leave an earlier investment standing in it, when tho proprietor has it in his power to reduce the best investment to mere waste paper, by taking advances on Bureau-security I And then, the administration of the Bureau, the only anchor lor creditors to repose faith in, how is that ?

Have we not seen that the esiential part thereof, the part on which the loan is contingent, lias been entrusted to some notoriously insolvent planters, who first and most of all needed such loans, although the ordinance quoted enacts in its 2, that they are to he two of the most respected and well-to-do Planters in the Island ? But, there is a secret in it, which I will tell, and that is, that if respected and conscientious wellto-do planters had that business, then those on the other side of that line would have narrower limits wherein to do their little niceties and they therefore take care to have the job given amongst themselves. It is time that all this should cease, and that the business as well as the credit of the Island should flow hack into their natural channels, and not any longer be buoyed up by artificial measures iuteuded for a former and different state of things. But first of all, it is high time that such loans from the Landtreasury should be put an end to. Tho Burgher-Council has not a shadow of right to dispose in that manner of the funds amassed by taxes upon the Inhabitants, and tho individual members of that Council have even less right to portion out these funds among themselves. If they must keep up an Institution of the kind, and if they must borrow money on a security, which by right and justice should belong to their other creditor, then, at least, let them get the money elsewhere, and not lay their hands on what belongs to their Constituents,
the taxpayers, who never have, and probably never will consent, to that employment theroof.

Hitherto, particular circumstances have happened opportunely to prevent losses which would if the measure is persisted in, it is always, clear but this will surely uot ho tho case Landtreasury otherwise have occurred to the quite and' ; that there must and will he losses. Besides, the public funds are not intended to constitute a Bank, rior to he used for what is positively nothing else than a banking business, and that even an unsafe business, subject to much risk and great loss and no gain. There is at the present moment public Buildings here tumbling down for want of repairs, which repairs have for years been pressed upon the notice of the Burgher-Council as indispensably necessary, aud acknowledged as such by this Council. Yet, they cannot he done, because the means, although at hand, are applied or intended by the Council for loans principally to its own members. How different it would be, if by a clean sweep all the insolvent members were, as they should be, driven out of the Council. It will bo a great good luek, if none of tho money is lost this year, and there should then he made an end to tire system. And it must bo hoped that the lenders, who pay 6 per cent Interest, will also be made to repay the 3 per cent more, which the Landtreasury had to pay to the Banks as discount tor money borrowed tor tire purpose of lending it to planters, a most absurd proceeding indeed, and not only absurd, hut unwarrantable aud actually reckless, and it would be just as unwarrantable if, as it is said,
this difference, is charged to the public expense, thus letting the Public pay the piper. But the Public must be a great fool, or it would net stand all this nonsense any longer.
26th April 18ti0.

To the Editor of the " St. Croix Avis" Dear Sir ! In your paper of 24th inst., the article from the pen of Mr. Heilbuth, proves to me aud T would suppose to the whole community, hat our press is quite tree enough ; when in its columns, veiy worthy, hard working men, an held up to ridicule and contempt : and a anions charge, brought against the electoral committee of tlie colonial council, or somebody connected with the election, which I do not quite understand; and also, against the highest authority. Is not tlrcD the press as tree as it ought to be : The last paragraph of the article, regarding the lending of money on Bureau-certificate, is ridiculous, absurd, splenetic : is not money borrowed, and lent, all over the world? And although the most wealthy, may be necessitated at certain periods to borrow, 1 expect it is generally, needy persons who do so Do not the banks lend money? Certainly not on better security than the Burgher Council receives. I consider it as great an accommodation to the Burgher Council, as it is to the needy planter, to receive interest for money that would he laying idle in their chest ; therefore, it is nraki g money, instead of being locked up ; it is working for the benefit of the public : how their c;.n Mr. Heilbuth assert it is a " pernicious principle," it is no recent system, as lie would try make us believe. The Burgher Council has been lending to the planters, as long as I recollect ; and the government has shewn, not only a kind feel

ing, towards the planting interest, which supports all and every body here (even Mr. Heilbuth) hut great prudence in sanctioning such loans. Let me assuro the gentleman that I have known many worthy men saved from ruin ; by loans from the Burgher i ouncil. I have not the slightest bad feeling towards Mr. Heilbuth, quite the reverse. He " appears to insinuate his desire to protect the taxpaying public." Not all the logic that ho is master of, will make tho public believe, that he cares one fig for their interest. The observations he has already made about lending the public money, don't come very well from him. Whether Mr. Heilbuth, takes any notice of my observations or not, you will never hear again from rnc on tho subject. I have stated only plain facts. What I particularly wish, is, that the Govern mcnt would give him something to do. Yours truly, Moderator.

"Is not then the press as tree as it oujht to be ?" lie enquires. Moderator might have obtained an answer to his question trout the many recollections which, undoubtedly, must be treasured " up in his mind. It is a burlesque 011 the word freedom'' if applied to a press which, by law, is under censorship. No matter that the power of the censor is mildly swayed by a liberal-minded man, yet that power exists, and Moderator knows that it has often been exercised. The spirit of the times almost prevents its exercise : and this furnishes a powerful argument why it should bo abolished. The Press in these Polonies is therefore in an anomalous position ; aril this, Moderator will please oh serve, is the object which the public has in view by its agitation for the freedom of the press, viz : to hove its position fixed by law in accordance with Ike spirit of the times .

From the London Times. It is the fate of tyrianny to move blind and spellbound to destructon. Cruelty begets terror, and terror in turn impels to cruelty, until at last the madness of oppression reaches such a height that human nature can no longer endure it. There is a point of suffering at which the most slavish learn a les-on of manliness. Even supposing a community isolated from every other, and exposed without sympathy or assistance fiotn its neighbours to the extreme of wrong, we may be sure that there is a point which the ruler cannot pasi, and that either a revolution of the streets, as in France, or a revolution of the palace, as in ancient Rome and modern Russia, will bring relief to the opprersed. Still fairer are the hopes of a people whoso evil case is known and is the subject of astouisl.nient and indignation over all tlm world In ttie pres ut age it is impossible that even the most despotic Sovereigns can continue for ever to abuse their authority. In spite of all precautions, loreign ideas and foreign emissaries enter, and the ill-governed population are encouraged to a resistance before which in the end even the boldest King or Minis or must quail. It this were not so, the recent intelligence from Naples would carry despair to every heart. The state of that unfortunate country seems r ow to have arrived at its very worst The young King is surpassing his father in bigotry and cruelty. The unhappy Neapolitans have been relieved f rom Tiberius only to find Caligula. As the freedom of C oitr.il Italy has beeu assur-

ed, the tetror and violence of the Neapolitan Government have rcacht d suoh a point that it is difficult to believe in the perfect sanity of the King and bis agents. In R >tue the Papal Government has committed many excesses, but Cardinal Antonelli is a mild and philosophic ruler in comparison with the Neapolitan Mintsteis. In every letter the capital is described us subjected to a perfect reign of terror In the heated imagination of the King the voting of the people of Central Italy is to be the signal for a rising in the I'wo Sicilies. The advance of the Piedmrntese troops into Tuscany and the Romagna will, according to the Neapolitan politicians, bo followed hy an outbreak of all the Revolutionists in the States of the Church and in Central Italy. The only means of averting this catastrophe is to get rid of every leading Revolutionist, Ills Majesty " Revolutionist" and " Liberal" and, as in the mind of are convertible terras, the most extraordinary measures ate being taken in the chief cities of the kingdom. The state of the capital has hern fully described in our late correspondence from Naples. It is nearly four years since the

$ 0 $ Qj o X & y/ Q su excesses of the Government determined the English aud French Sovereigns to withdraw their representatives, but this step, being followed hy no active measures, has beeu totally disregarded by the Court of Naples. The representatives of the two countries are now the powerless spectators of crimes far greater than I those which moved the auger of Napoleon and of Lord Palmerston's Government in 1850. Their advice is not asked, and it is coldly received when they volunteer it. The proceedings of the police are scarcely covered by the decent veil of secrecy ; either the extremity of alarm or a cynical coutcmpt for public opinion causes them to disregard all appearances and to outrage every human right in the face of day. As is well known, the Neapolitan Government has been long intent on getting rid of every man of statiou or culture who is supposed to be infected with liberal opinions. It seems to have come to the conclusion that its own existence is incompatible with any degree of thought or aspiration in the people. Every mail of education who does not form part of the machine of State is suspected of disaffection, and it may he said to he on him to prove his loyalty hy some servile act or some display of open partisanship with the ruling powers For some time past the process of weeding out all iudependeut-iniuded lneu has bei 11 going on, and by threats or actual expulsiou a number of the most eminent citizens of Naples hayo been bauished from their country. Within the last

few weeks, however, this process has increased in intensity. Men are suddenly arrested, aud( without the proof of auy crime, even without an accusation, they are bunied to prison, or placed ou board ship to be sent out of the country. Not one heie and there, not merely souio busy correspondent of the Tuscan or I'iedmoutese Liberals, not merely some incautious talker at a cafe, but men of quiet lives and reserved ch aracter, men of professional 1 eminence, averse from violent changes, anj only anxious for some abatement of the cruelty and fetocity of the Gov rnment, are suddenly seized and Lurried awav, often widiout permission to communicate with their families. The deportations arc sometimes made in mass. Our correspond lit writes that a few days since 14 persons were seized to be sent out of the country, and ill seven cas s the sentence was actually executed. Among them were 111, 11 of the highest rank, and the only explanation which the police deigned to give was that their residence in Naples was incompatible with public tranquility. But banishment is not the worst fate which can befall a Neapolitan Liberal. In Paris or London lie lives a lit e man, lie may hope to be presently joined hy his wife and children, and he looks forward to the day when the present tyranny will he overthrown, or the ruler taught moderation hy misfortune or the remonstrance of his neighbours. To the victim who is immured in one of the dungeons of

the police no sucli consolations come. Ho must undergo the extremity of misery, oppressed by dirt, foul smells, villa 0.1s food, the insolence of gaolors, the society of the most infamous, and, if report speaks true, even the torture of the lash. His health in iy be ruined, and deliverance inay come too late to res oie him to his former self. This punishment is n<>w inflicted on men against whom there is nothing more than a shadow of susp cion Happy the man who only remains in these iufected cells for a few days, or until his banishment ; has been decided upon ! The terror at present prevailing in Naples is said to surpass anything 1 even in the gloomy annals of the late reign. No one cau doubt that these monstrous crimes are sure to produce the very cousequeuces they are intended 'to avert. After all, the Neapolitans are Italians, and though, perhaps,

not so gifted intellectually as their northern countrymen, they have quick feelings, and, when roused, a fair amount of energy. If Machiavel had been the adviser of the young King, he would assuredly have advised him to make common cause with the Sardinian Monarch, and establish his power in Southern Italy by the same course which has made his rival the head of a great kingdom in the North. The folly of attempting to shut out the influences which now reign at Florence and Bologna must be evident to every mind not trained by the priests, courtiers, and the most ignorant of women. The King of Naples might, without parting with a shred of his power, without even giving a Constitution, have made himself a popular King, and held the balance between Sardinia and t be Papacy. The merest concessions to natural justice, the abandonment of il system shocking to the most retrograde politicians in Europe, the restraining of a police against whose doings even Austria has protested, might have assured King Francis the opening of a prosperpus and powerful reign. But a blindness which may be called judicial shuts out t lie path of honour and success. It would be a libel 011 humanity to suppose that his Go: comment can remain unchanged. The day of retribution is probably at hand, and another Royal fugitive may soon give that warning to Kings which has been so often repeated in our times. o Exclusion of Reporters from the Houses of Parliament The year 1771 opened (writes William Howitt, in " Cas-

sell's Illustrated History") under circumstances which greatly diminished the interest in Parliamentary proceedings. As all reporting was excluded from the House of Lords, the chief speakers then felt that they were no longer addressing the nation, but merely a little knot of persons in a corner, and consequently the stimulus of both fame and real usefulness was at an end. Chatham says, in a letter : þÿ "The house being kept clear of hearers, we are reduced to a snug party of unhearing and unfeeling lords, and the tapestry hung up." In the Commons, the desire of the Ministry to reduce that popular arena to the same condition of insignificance produced a contest with the City as foolish and mischievous in its degree as the contests then going 011 with Wilkes and America. George Onslow, nephew of the late .Speaker, and member for Guildford, moved that several printers, who had dared to report the debates of the House of Commons, should be summoned to the bar to answer for their conduct. Accordingly these mediums of communication betwixt the people and their representatives were summoned and reprimanded on their knees. One of their number, named Miller, however declared that lie was a liveryman of London, and that any attempt to arrest him would be a breach of the privileges of the City. The Serjeant-at-Arms dispatched a messenger to apprehend this sturdy citizen, and bring liini before the House ; but, instead of succeeding, the parliamentary messenger was taken by a City constable, and carried be-

fore Brass Crossby, the Lord Mayor. With the Lord Mayor sate Alderman Wilkes and Alderman Oliver. It was delightful work to Wilkfs thus to set at defiance the House of Commons, which had made such fierce war 011 him. The Lord Mayor, accordingly, was fully confirm d in his view þÿ that the messenger of the Commons had committed a flagrant violation ot the City charter, in endeavouring to lay hands on one of its liverymen within its own precincts, and they held the messenger accordingly to bail.

We are indebted to Mr. Cliegaryn, of the Thames Admiralty Agent, for some information, and a Vera Cruz paper of the 1st April, concerning the siege of that town by Miramon, tho chief of one of the rival factions, contending for the possession of the Mexican Gevernmont. Miramon þÿ i s s the Clerical party, and opposed to the views and alliance with the United States. Tho Veracruzanos having incurred his hostility, probably from the exhibition of a disposition favorable to the rival faction, be resolved upon

besieging the City, and on the 4th March made bis appearance before tho walls. From the 4th to the 13th was passed in entrenching his forces, which consisted of some 5000 men, placing his batteries, and making preparations to open fire. On the 13th he entered into a conference with the town authorities, which whs continued to the next day, and proving fruitless, on the morning of the 15th the bombardment began. It continued for seven days and was directed chiefly against the buildings of tho town. The first shot struck the Church, the second fell upon the French Consulate. Captain Aldham of H. M. S. Valorous, sent to Miramon to protest against this proceeding, which lie described as contrary to the rules of civilised warfare. Miþÿramon s object appears to have been to strike terror into the inhabitants by the destruction of their houses, and so compel a surrender. From the smallness of his force and the strength of the defences he was prevented from attempting an assault. He protected his forces behind a sand' hill, beyond which he placed mortars and threw bombs into the town without any risk. By this means he endeavoured to set fire to the town, the bombs being filled with inflammable stuff ; but as soon as any of the roofs were observed to take fire, it was extinguished by the citizens. Bat Miramon was in expectation of a supply of arms and ammunition which had been procured for him from the Havana by Marin in twosteamers the Concepcion and the Marquis, which being observed from the torn lying off, and

showing no flag, they were suspected, and followed by the U. S. ship-of-war Saratoga , which fired into them and seized them. This was a death blow to þÿMiratnou s hopes. His powder failing him, þÿMarin s ships and supplies being seized and carried away to the States, and the bombardment producing no other effect but exasperation upon the townsfolk, Miramon abandoned the siege on the night of the 22nd, leaving behind some of his guns, and moved off with all celerity to Jalapa. It is said that during the siege he threw from 5 to 600 bombs and about 4000 shot into the town, but the loss of life officially reported did not exceed 7 killed and 37 wounded amongst the garrison, and 13 killed in the city. The damage to houses, however, was considerable, estimated at a million of dollars. 1 o account for the trifling loss of life, ir. should be added, that previous to the commencement of the bombardment a large portion of the inhabitants, chiefly of the women and children, had sought refuge in the ships in the harbour, and amongst the neighbouring villages, which wero not molested by the enemy. The authorities sent a great number of poor persons (about 2000) in two vessels, which they employed for the purpose of conveying them, to Alvarado and Tlacotalpam, where they also furnished them with provisions. Whilst Miramon was engaged in the siege, the Bishop of Mexico, it is said, offered up prayers for his success, and formed a procession of hundreds of women through tho principal streets chanting prayers

all along the way. þÿMiramon failure, s however, cannot but prove a great disaster to his party; his army had suffered severely, it is said to the extent of two filths. There were rumors of his resigning the command to Robles. It is not at all improbable that the next accounts will be the discomfiture of his party, and the installation of Juarez and the Liberal party in tho supremo power at Mexico. o þÿ Negro Wit. þÿ The Steamer Esk having arrived at St. Thomas, a bontman exclaimed þÿ þÿ Eh-eh! dem call dis X: þÿ we hab de Y ; (Wye) by and by we go hab de Z !

In reporting on t e d aft of the Budget for the Danish W stimlia Possessions, for the year fr in the 1st April 1860 to the 31st March 1861, tlie Colonial Council considers it its duty, on account of the special occasion now offered, in the first place, to express its opinion, both as to the conditions under which the present draft has been laid before the Council, and, generally, as to the present state of the colonies. Tin Council must express its regret, that a perit d of near four years has passed since the last se-sion of the Council, so that three financial years have passed without an opportunity being given to the representative body of the islands to exercise that influence vested in th in by the Colonial-law, respecting the financial and the other affairs of these communities, for the development and furtherance of which tlie action of the Council is a constitutional condition ; and further, that this Council expects, that a neglect of the enactment contained in the law of 26th Mareh 1852 23 respecting the annual convocation of the Colonial Council will in future not he repeated. As to the present state of the colonies generally, the Council cannot omit pointing out, that the islands, and especially St. Croix, having, during the 11 years lapsed since the emancipation, had to contend with the troubles and difficulties caused by ibis event, great sacrifices have b. en made to procure the very considerable means required for effecting the impr ivements made necessary by the novel cir-

cumstances ; the last three years have been so unfavorable as regards the sugar-production, that the revenue lias scarcely covered the ordin i y expenditure of cultivation, while the const ant and alarming aliiniuution of labor has rendered it imperatively necessary to prepare the obtaining of means for importing foreign labor-rs, in order to counteract the danger threatening the most important source of revenue. The interests of St. Thomas have during the same period been likewise severely affected by the sundry circumstances, especially by the changes in the commercial action and policy of other natious, which threaten gradually to withdraw the commerce from the island. Under such circumstances the Council feels every inducement to endeavor, to effect as far as possible a reduction and a moro proper apportioning of the burthens most pressing on the principal interests and on the community at largo ; and as regards the expenditure, to propose every reduction, that may bo effected by judicious economy ; also without reserve to express its views relative to any measures, by which the costly administration may be euableu to secure the dispatch of publio business, to obtain obedience to the laws and to advance the development of general interests. Proceeding to give our views respecting the special sections of the draft, we would, as regards the Revenue repeat the þÿCouncil general s remark to the draft of the Budget for 1856-57, rolative to the expediency of a revision of the

system of taxation, whereby several of the present taxes, which in consequence of thn late changes have become oppressive and unfair, may be replaced by others, calculated for the present state of things, and more equally »p portioned to the ability of the interests concerned.

In determining the pi ice. the freight is of course an important item, and the existing double export duty must in a g cat measure make the articles dearer, when th inip rti rs cannot secure to the vessels bringing cargo s any returnfreight, but such vessels have to look for returnfreight somewhero else Besides it þÿ prevents the access to this island ( floating- j entirely þÿcargoes, so advantageous to other West India islands, vessels bringing out cargoes lor their own account, in order to purchase for the proceeds return-cargo of Westindia produce, a traffic which naturally cannot be expected where the cargo to be exported would be burdened with an extra impost of about 6 per cent. N E A POUT AN N EGOTI ATIONS. Turin, June 12. By ratifying an armistice between Geueral Lanzi and Garibaldi, the King of Naples has removed the principal obstacle which prevented foreigu mediation. From the moment that the Kiog of Naples treats with the Sicilian revolu-

S T. MO I. X, A V I S . tionary party as one Power with another, mediation becomes possible without infringing upon I diplomatic formalities. This explains the sending of the Commander de Martino to Paris, who is charged, on the part of Francis II., to submit the bases aud the guarantees for the personal mediation repeatedly invoked by his Majesty from Napoleon III. Although authorising the Com- j tuander de Martino to come to Paris, the Emperor of the French reserves to himself the liberty of not coming to a decision until after having received positive overtures from of the the Neapolitan At all events, the Court Tuileries does not envoy. wish to undertake any mediation unless in concert with England aud with the other great Powers. The following are the bases on which the King of Naples conseuts, as least for the present, to an arrangement with the Sieiliau insurrectionists :- Fraucis II. is ready to engage himself to grant a liberal constitution on the broadest bases to Sicily, to be also applied to the whole Kingdom. Should the Sicilians desire a distinct and independent existence, the King would extend his concessions so far as to place Sicily iu a position similar to that of the Duchy of Duxetnburg. The attitude of Count Cavour leaves, however, little hope of a solution favourable to the King of Naples. Garibaldi being triumphant, Count Cavour now requests the Cabinet of the Tuileries to adopt, iu regard to Sicily, the policy lollowed in reference to Tuscany, Parma, M"dcna, and the Legations. This request has only been con-

j fidentially made to the Emperor Napoleon. Count Cavour has addressed an official dispatch to the Chevelier Nigra, who communicated its conteuts to M. Thouvenel about four days ago. In this dispatch Count Cavour expresses a hope that France will not in any way interfere in the affairs of Sicily. He reminds the French Cabinet that the principle of non-intervention in Italy, as contained in the celebrated note ol Lord John Russell, lias been officially accepted by the French Government.

From the London Times , June 15. SARDINIA AND SICILY (FROM THE TIMES' t'ORRKSPONDENT.) Turin, June 12. These are anxious moments for Italy, and every soul is busy with conjectures as to impending contingencies. If this long-despised nation were only for once allowed fair play, the word " non-intervention'' admitted of any if it were suffered to work out its own destinies, if other definition than that given by Talleyrand, there would not be one man here entertaining the least doubt as to the final is<ue. Garibaldi has achieved what every man in his senses looked upon as an impossibility þÿ what the epic narrative of your Palermo correspondent demonstrated to every man's satisfaction to have been an utter impossibility. So long as that King of Pate is allowed freedom of action, wonders of the same nature will never cease. By the time I am writing all Sicily is his, with the exception of the citadel of Messina. Before the end of a month all Naples will equally be his, with the exception, perhaps, of the stronghold of Gaeta. He only lacked aims and ammunition. By this time Medici has, in all probability, landed with the warlike stores, without which Garibaldi had already achieved half his work. The human material was all this time at hand. The Sicilians are, or may be, made into fighting-men. Weie they even insufficient or inefficient, Medici already brings with him 2,000 well-tried combatants, able officers, crack shots, dare-devil adventurers. Were the struggle to assume more important dimensions, there are here, in Genoa, at Leg-

horn, 40,000 youths burning to join in the melee. The Neapolitans have shown but little fighting, and are weary of it. Either from cowardice or patriotism, they will soon give up the game. Expeditions to the Abruzzi and Calabria are everywhere being planned Before Garibaldi allows himself one day's rest of the smoking ruins of Palermo he will have laid his plans for carrying the war into the mainland. The Royal fleet has virtually lost the command of the sea ; communications are everywhere open ; the smallest craft can land its freight on any part of the coast of both kingdoms with hardly any dodge or concealment. The patriots show themselves and conquer, cause alone. The cry is " Italian union and and their victory leads to the success of one Victor Emmanuel !" There is no fear of division of counsel, or of divergence of scopo. Mazzini is going or gone to Sicily, but will be unable to do mischief. His best old friends, Medici, Cosenz, Sirtori, and Bixio, are determined to set him aside as an unpractical, dangerous bungler. Garibaldi will lay Hold of him tenderly, and ship him off to Montevideo or the Antipodes. He has inti listed his Government to La Farina, a man who enjoys the confidence of Count Oavour ; so that the Italian movement obeys the impulse of one leading miud þÿ that of avast, bold, wary, deep scheming mind. Uudor La Farina are Torre-Arsa, Michele Amari, and other illustrious Sicilians, who are the very reverse of Republicans. Crispi, La Masa, and others are reclaimed Maz-

zinians ; they have embraced anti-M izzinian views with the proverbial zeal of converts. The instinct of union among the Italians of the present day is the greatest prodigy of the age | Remove all foreign obstacles, and the nation will go straight to its aim in the most unflinching, uncompromising way. But, alas! but, alas! are theie no foreign rocks ahead ? Here the opinion of the Italians is bomewkat divided. The Sardinian Government, so far as I can make out þÿ for, remember, I am not and do not wish to be in their confidence, lest my connexion with them should interfere with my office as an independent and impartial observer þÿ this Government and their partisans are as sanguino as men may well be. They have full faith in the non-intervention of the Great Powers. Had it not beeu for the blundering camisade of that unlucky, priestslaying Zambianchi, they have no doubt but the Emperor of the French would by this time have fulfilled his oft-repeated promise to remove the French garrison from Rome and all the Roman State. If, they justly argue, Napoleon III. abandons tho Pope to bis fate, 1 much more will he leave the Neapolitan Bourbnn to his own devices Deprived of French | support, the Pope is now in worse straits than

t ® (?) ri ft' 1j & 0 % « he was before Lamoricifire became '' Soldato del Papa " His Holiness applied for money the other day, and the banker Torlonia, after asking free leave of speech, pointed out to him where money was to be found, charging Cardinal Autouelli with the very recent embezzlement of eight millions of money. Presently Cardinal Wiseman brought the same charge against the Secretary of Slate ; the Pope turned his buck spitefully upon the plain-spoken banker and the blunt English prelate, and would hear never a word against the man who, either through love or fear, has completely enj thralled the Holy Father. Wisemau came j was heard to say it was full time to bow to from the audience completely crestfallen, and ' the hand of Providence, by which the downfall of the temporal power was visibly decreed." The ruin of the Papacy and of the Bourbon sway has, then, come to pas, say these hopeful patriots ; and no foreign hand will be stretched out to avert if. Meanwhile, what say the men whose confidence does not so readily keep pace with their wishes? j Why, in their judgment, Napoleon's mind is an inscrutable gulf. He may be unable to carry j out his original design, but he is not willing to i relinquish it to the last. His object was and is, not the deliverance of Italy, bat its subjection, direct or indirect, to France. The primitive at its head the Pope a mere passive tool in the plan was an þÿ Italian Conle.deracy, with the Pope hands ol France, presiding over a Diet of Italian States, whose conflicting views and interests al-

lowed France a supreme control over their discordant delibeiations. Sardinia, enlarged in the east, but weakened in the west, was to exercise no power except in obedience to French ascendancy. With that view Austria, though crippled and effete, was allowed to keep up a menacing attitude in the heart of Loiubardy. The spirit cd conduct of Central Italy compelled the Emperor so far to depart front his piogramme as to abandon the cause of Dtlkes and Grand Dukes, aud gave rise to the notion of an Italian triuitya division of the country into thieo States of the North, Centre, and South. Farini, Ricasoli, Favour, and still more Bologna and Florence, defeated evin that scheme, aud now we have been led to the new idea of an Italian duality, or id' two great kingdoms, at. Turin and Naples. Is j Garibaldi to be allowed to baffle eveu this last, project ? Suppose Garibaldi can manage forward, with all Europe looking on, " Pat me au to push bras;" behold Naples and Sicily made one with Piedmont. Lombardy, T uscany, and the /Emilia ; behold Victor Emmanuel crowned on the emancipated Capitol, with the Pope either at Jerusalem, at Avignon, or even at the Vatican, but only as Bishop of Bishops ; and behold the alternative offered to Austria, either of selling Venice against all the gold, the pictuies, statues, and manuscripts with which gold may be made, or else challenged to a struggle in which all the youth of Italy will be brought to sit i.i arms for 10 years round the fortresses of the Quadilateral,

as before so many Troys; and the Italian race j will be re-tempered aud regenerated by a struggle renewing the exploits and sacrifices of the old wars of the Lombard League! Is this what Napoleon wants? Is it what he wanted when he proclaimed at Milan that the Italians must all be soldiers that they might all become free men, or when he declared that Frauce had accomplished her task, and the rest inu.-t be left to the Italians themselves? Undoubtedly, the moment has come when Italy can 'far da sc.' A couple of charges with the bayonet by a handful of "Filibusters" has complotely turned the scale both against her home tyrants and against that co ossal Power which was hitherto h.-r only foreign oppressor. Let us, then, see the effect, of two more such charges with the Gaiibaldun bayonets. Will Napoleon 'laisser laire?' We hear of the Toulon fleet sailing to Naples We hear of the Commendator De Martino travelling post- ! haste to the Tuileries. We hear þÿ ominous news þÿ that the lion-intervention is limited to Sicily. It is an old trick of the French press to throw all the blame of an intervention upon Eugland, as a pretext to justify the intervention of France. They trumped up the telegram au. uouncing the occupation of Palermo by the English Admiral, whereas tho cruel truth was that no man stepped forward, even in vindication of the common cause of humanity, to prevent the dastardly Royal troops from laying Palermo in ashes. Interference against the Bourbon no foreign Power attempts; will there equally be no
i meddling in his favour? The question lies now

in a nutshell. Is Victor Emmanuel to be King of Italy, or is Napoleon to be Emperor of the French and protector of two great Italian kingdoms? Is Italy to be a uation, or is she to become the handmaiden of France ? There is hardly a man 1 know in the world more intimately than De Martino. He is a Liberal, and the son of a Liberal. The old King Ferdinand always valued aud employed him as a thoroughly honest man, whose patriotic notions might be inconvenient in the immediate neighbourhood of the Court, hut who could and should always be trusted with any delicate mission abroad which required skill and dexterity, and did not involve abnegation of honour aud principle. On his deathbed the ruthless tyiaut bequeathed the able diplomatist to his sott sh sou, bidding him turn to De Martino in all cases of serious complication aud distress. If auy man can save the Bourbon Monarchy, it is I)e Matiuo alone; and he is at this very moment exerting his extremely versatile talents to that effect. De Martino is an avowed dualist; he harbours invincible Piedmontese antipathies, and he will give ' carte-blanclie' to France if she will either uphold the Southern State under its present Sovereign, or under any other Prince or dynasty, at his own (the Emperor's) choice. Will Napoleon III. resist the temptation? Will h , iu deference to national Italian tendencies, abaudon a plan which coincides with his | longcherisbed views? Will he not preler a I dualism which prolongs the existence of the tot-

tering Papacy, which gives France a chance of exercising the functions of a Moderai ir iu Italy, to an ltaliuu uuity which always seemed monstrous to him, which clashed with all his preconceived notioni, upset all his long-laid plans, and places Italy in a position to obey the behests of France only in so far as they suit her own pleasure and convenience, and no farther ? Momentous questions are these, and J who moot themam too happy to think that my duty as a newsman by no means compels me to answer or solve them. 1 shall have done enough, I think, if 1 acquaint English readers with the conflicting surmises of the great party leaders in this ItaliaD movement, all of whom equal y aspiie to a united' Italian nationality, hut some ol whom confidently assert, and perhaps beliete, that the attainment of this object lies with themselves alone ; whilo others think that they will have to settle accounts with foreign Powers, and especially with Franco þÿ with that. France who w ill not favour their unitarian views, and will not even limit herself to a policy of neutrality and iioii-iuterveutiou.

Froiu the N. O Delta of June, 25. Highly interesting IVom thofiiilf. THE CAPTURE OF ANOTHER NAMELESS SI.AVER þÿ FULL AND MINUTE PARTICULARS OF THE CHASE. U. S. S. Crusader, May 27, 1860. As the U. S. steamer Crusader was eruising in the old Bahama Chatiuel, not far from Neuvitas, on the 23d of May, a square-rigged vessel of moderate size was reported fiom aloll. We immediately stood lor her, as no sail is allowed to pass us in these slaver-hunter waters, or even to come in sight, without having her character ascertained. As soon as she lound herself an object of pursuit, the strange sail began to behave in such a manner as strongly excited our suspicions, and at length put her helm up and ran in for the shore, thus taking the last and most desperate chauce ot escape. U u fortunately for her, the wind was so light that she was prevented from effecting her purpose, and we rapidly overhauled her, notwithstanding that she was eairying all her canvas The Crusader now hoisted English colors and fired a gun to windward, when after some delay, the bark (for such she pioved to be) finally displayed tbe French flag at the peak. By this time, however, we were so near ihat we were enabled to see that her hatches were all closely covered over, and as we contiuued to approach, we could even distinguish at intervals the peculiarly loathsome odor of a crowded slave-ship. TTnd r these circumstances it was determined to board her, and accordingly a treat and the English ensign were lowered at the same time, and

the American colors were hoisted. No sooner did the Crusader's boat leave her side than the bark hauled down the French colors, and, a< we subsequently learned, threw them and their Portuguese papers overboaid together ; so that when she was boarded she had neither papers nor colors, and was cuiifessidly without oauie or nationality. For a little while there was dead silence ou board both ships, though the increasing strong ammoniacal African odor placed beyond all doubt the fact that the bark had under her hatches a cargo of negroes And now we begau to hear a sort of suppressed moaning, which soon swelled into the unmistakable murmur of human voices. As our boat reached the side of the bark, and the officer in charge sprang ou the deck, with n tremendous shout the hatches were forced open from below, and out burst hundreds, the self-liberated slaves. As they caught sight of the stars and stripes floating so near þÿ which no doubt seemed to these poor wretches like a bright rainbow of promise þÿ they became perfectthe i a i I þÿ ly frantic with joy They el mbed þÿ they hung on the shrouds they clust- up all along i red like swarming bees in the rigging, while rose from sea to sky the wildest acclamations of delight. They danced, and leaped, and waved their aims in the air, and screamed, and yelled in a discordant but pathetic concert. There was one thing, however, even more touching than all this outcry of barbaric rejoicing. My attention was attracted to a group consisting of some-

what more than a hundred women, withdrawn apart from the shouting and noisy men. Their behavior was in strong contrast with that of the others, and was characteristic of their sex. Entirely nude, but innocently UDahashed, they sat or knelt in tearful and silent thanklulness. Several of them held infants in their arms, and through their tears, liko sunshine from behind a cloud, beamed an expression of the deepest gratitudo and happiness. The men looked as though they had just been raised from espair to the most exultant gladness The scene of confusion on board the bark, when the negroes found themselves released

% t. e s o b i ti » s % frotn the accustomed restraint baffles all description They had, of course, all been kept ou a very small allowance of food and water during the passage. The first use they made of their liberty was to satisfy their hunger and thirst, wliicii they did by breaking into tbe bread barrels and water-casks, and then running about eating, drinking, dancing, and screaming, all at once. It mattered hut little to them what sort of vessels they drank þÿfrom buckets, boxes, and troughs were ail brought into requisition. I even saw several fellows, happy and delighted, with a piece of bread in one hand and a wooden spitton lullot muddy water in were As soon as their appetites the other. satisfied, the African fondness for finery began to show itself, aud all the loose articles in the ship were employed as personal ornaments. Some fastened belaying pins to their wrists, aud sotne strutted proudly about with copper ladles hung round their necks. By this time, however, a detachment of marines arrived from the Crusader, aud order was at onee restored, and an organization established. The negroes were clothed with pieces of canvas, and the captain, -supercargo and crew, sent ou board the Crusader as prisoners. They made no claims or remonstrances whatever, but surrendered themselves as slavers, without nationality. They stated that the bark had no name, aud i hat all their papers had been thrown overboard with the colois. They seemed to bear their loss with philosophic equanimity. Such a contingency had evidently been regarded

by them as part of their risk, aud they were not unprepared for it. The captain is a Frenchman, as is also the supei cargo, and the crew are mostly Spaniards, with a few Frenchmen. '1 he negroes were selected from among 3,000 prisoners of war recently taken by the King of Duhoiuey. They were brought frotn Wliydah, a large town ou the slave coast, in the Bight ol Benin, the sea-port of the renowned Kingdom of Dahomey. They ate much superior to the Congos, who u.-ually compose the cargoes of slavers, not only in physique but also in intelligence Nearly all arc in cxccllcut health, which is no doubt owing to the careful arrangements made for their comfort on board the bark. In number they amount to about 450; and the slave deck affords ample accommodation for them all. During a passage of 45 days from the Gulf of Guinea, seveu only have died, which is certainly a very small number. The passage from Cuba to Key West was made without auy deaths among the negroes, and without any incident ot iuterest. Baracoons have been erected at Key V\ est lor tbe accommodation of re-captured slaves, and our cargo will be sent thither as soon as possible. The prisoners will remain in charge of the II. S. Marshal, to await the result of their trial. This is the first prize captured by the Crusader since she has been in the gull. It is proper to state that this is not to be attributed to any waut of activity or efficiency on the part of this cruiser, but is due to the fact that she has been

kept a greater part of the time away frotn the station. On her first arrival in the Gulf, she found herself dispatched by her sealed orders up the Mississippi, to iutercept a suspected filibuster expedition, and was detained by instructions from the Government at anchor off New Orleans for nearly two months. Subsequently, she was again compelled to leave the coast ot Cuba for the purpose ot having a new deck laid at Pensacola, which involved another month of absence. And on a third occasion, just when several cargoes were expected, an accident to her machinery obliged her to go to Key West for repairs, at the time that the Wildfire and the William were captured by the Mohawk and Wyandotte She is even now in a partially disabled condition, on account of a broken cyliuder, which it is impossible to repair perfectly, and which should be immediately replaced by a new one. In Barbados, be it observed, our land has no rtst þÿ the field from which the caDes are cut in April or May is immediately (most likely) planted with potatoes which yield a heavy crop þÿ and then prepared for receiving the cane plants about the next Christmas, and yet you see, notwithstanding this hardwork, it has increased in fertility as shown by an average of

crops. It is further to be remarked that no two Islands are so much alike as Barbados and St. Croix. 1 do not think we have any advantage any way þÿ except perhaps in one district, now not so fertile as it used to be. I have thus, my dear Sir, endeavoured to lay before you some of the many conditions which may lead you to modify the system of cultivation and also to encourage you to hope to seo much better duys. I would beg of you in conclusion to observe that our two piaciiees differ very materially, and that the results differ no less þÿ surely we cannot but decide in favour of tbe system accompanied by the best results. If I should have succeeded in enabling you to come to an advantageous conclusion, I shall be most happy. I need scarcely say that I do not mean to arrogate to myself the least degree of superiority to your St. Croix planters I dare say they would manage an Estate much better than I could do, but it often happens that a bystander studying the game sees what the players overlook. 1 hope I shall not have wearied you. If you like to show this to any one you are quite at liberty to do so. With best wishes, Yours truly, P. L. PHILLIPS. To the Editor of the "Avis." Proximua ardct U calegou. V irg. On Tuesday next an election of a member to serve in the Burgher Council will take place. Have your readers no intention to return such a member as will help to clear away till those abuses which have crept into our political institutions? lias our climate so bane-

ful tin influence as to produce all that apathy of mind and body which we see around us on questions of vital importance to this colony? In the name of our children, who will bear the inheritance of a country whose prosperity lias been irrecoverably lost, ought we not to look to the end of the state of things now existing, evincing, as it does, political corruption in its worst forms? I am aware that, the power of returning members is virtually in the hands of the planters alone. By the very narrow and unfair suffrage, three-fourths of the votes are in the hands of estate proprietors and their managers; which latter are saved the exhaustive mental labour to think for themselves, and the waste of their employers' time in writing their own votes, by having billets sent them by their employers, containingthe names of those whom these august oligarchs would have returned. Yet, is this a reason why no combined effort should he made to have that representation of a mixed nature, by returning some one who, while acknowleding that the planting interest is a great one in this Island, would still not lie inclined to sacrifice all other interests to that one alone? Inhabitants of this Island, and ye natives especially! Look well unto what you do; for the time will come when grovelling poverty will overspread this land, and when those possessed of other homes will retire from among you, leaving you to drag out a poverty stricken existence on an exhausted soil. Yours truly

St. CHRI3TIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 10th JULY, 1S60. A remarkable debate, or rather, conversation, is said to have taken place yesterday in the Burgher Council. As it is not probable that, three or four months hence, when the proceedings of this meeting are published, the public will receive any information of it, we undertake to furnish our readers with suchun account as has been related to us. Ou the 7th April last the Burgher Council advertised an amount of $600 to be lent out from the Ruinfund. Our establishment yielding no revenue beyond what is necessary to cover its expenses, and being in waut of a new stock of materials, we petitioned for the loan, offering security in the property of the proprietress of the establishment. The Burgher Council granted $400, on condition that the balance of a former loan, on the same security, be repaid. As this amount would (all far short of that required for the outlay, we again p.'titioncd the Council either to make up the 8600 required from the Landtreasury 's means, or to allow the amount granted us to remain until the full amount should have accumulated. This the Chairman declined to do, and notified to us that the amount refused by us would again be advertised. Before doing so, however, the Bookkeeper discovered that the Ruinfund could then dispose of $600 ; and on our requesting that our petition should now be taken into consideration, we were politely told that the amount would again be advertised and we might then renew our petition. This we did : and yesterday the Council decided the matter, not on the

merits of the several applicants, but, we regret to say, according to illiberal, narrow, and personal motives One of the leading members observed that he could not sec any uecessity to grant our petition, as the newspaper is made use of by anonymous and other writers to traduce the members of public institutions and the institutions themselves. He was, we are told, warmly taken up by other members who could not join him in refusing to grant the petition on this ground, as being subversive of the free expression of public opinion. A happy idea, a real inspiration, then took possession of the objector. He discovered that the petition was not " in form and then, by a strange inconsistency, our luke-warm friends voted away the money to others. On the question of " form," it will be necessary to observe that, our fiist petition offered security in property, and our last, merely referred to, and renewed the tcims of, the first one. It will appear to our readers, as it does to us, passing strange that the same security should in the one case, when the Council granted a part of the amount petitioned for, bo considered sufficient and consequently ''in form," but that alter the close of a few weeks (during which time a few anonymous articles against striking abuses in the Burgher Council appeared in this paper), that sumo petition should be considered "not in form !" We have thus briefly sketched the particulars of this interesting, and to the parties concerned, highly praiseworthy debate. One thing is

evident: we are made to suffer for the offences of our contributors, who seem to be beyond the reach of our worthy representatives Is not t his a confirmation of the assertion of our correspondents that, the Burgher Council is a faulty institution, whose members arc swayed more by passion, prejudice and self-interest than by reason and justice ? Is not this political corruption ? But the die is cast. If we are made the scape-goat on whioh the punishment for the sins of our correspondents is to be visited, we bow our head and submit. This outrage on public opinion may, no doubt, pass unnoticed, for of whom can we seek redress ? T wo courses are now left open to us to pursue, either one of which will, in these days of outward clamor for freedom of opinion, lead to our ruin. The one is the closing of our columns against every article except those in praise of our imperfect institutions. The other is to throw off all reserve, and, by an exposure of other abuses, prevent the spread of gangrene through our whole political system Will our readers direct us as to which course we should pursue'

Annexation to Honduras Officially Announced þÿ Great Indignation Declaration of Independence. þÿ Ruatan, May 22, 1860. The changes to which all parties here have been looking forward for the past few months with so much apprehension and anxiety, are now rapidly reaching their crisis. The news has been received for ionic time of the ratification of the treaty lately pending between Great Britain and the Honduras Government, hut the inhabitants of Ruatan and the other Bay Islands were not officially informed by the same until yesterday. His Excellency, Lieut. Gov Thos. Price, arrived here from Belize late on Saturday, and called a meeting yesterday, when the ratification of the convention was formally proclaimed. The inhabitants are very much dissatisfied with the terms of the treaty, and a committee of the most prominent of them was immediately formed to demaud certain privileges from Honduras accoiding to the Clarendon and Heran treaty of 1856, and should these not be conipliid with, will undoubtedly prepare for resistance. H. B. M 's officials, although in no way peisonally responsible for the change, must have felt themselves to be placed in a most painful and humiliating situation thus to transfer a fine and loyal body of subjects to iho rule of the despotic chief of a despotic republic. At the close of the meeting three cheers were given, but not in honor of the British Quern or British Government þÿ it was that the Anglo

Saxon institutions might prevail in all countries and climates, and among all colors. After making the disagreeable declaraiion, the Governor informed them, by way ot sw. etening the bitter pill, that the British Government would grant them lands in any of the West India colonics þÿ an offer that was refusi d. But it was suggested that Africa would be better for that pu-pose, for surely, the Monroe doctrine would not extend to that continent and it 8 dependencies, and, as it was likely to become a cotton-producing country, John Blight and the Manchester men would, for their own interest oppose any secessions that might he attempted there. A meeting was subsequently ealb d, and the question of declaring the independence ot the Bay Islands considered, and preliminary stops taken towards the formation ol a constitution. Nothing now remains in regard to the letter of the treaty, but the formal possession of the Bay Islands by the Honduras officials. There are a thousand flying rumors extant, upon which perfect reliance cannot be placed ; among these, that, the Honduras Government has made the Bay Islands subject to a system of espionage, and that, in the event of an outbreak, a large body of troops aic ready to entbatk and enforce the conditions of the treaty. The greatest excitement prevails, and it is difficult o fortcll the issue that will finally be reached. It is supposed that the Islands will be visited by the Honduras officials on the 28th inst , for the purpose of

hoisting their flag and taking formal possession. Proclamation by the Queen. Whereas, we have found ourselves constrained by paramount motives of State policy to separate the Islands of Ruatan, Utilla, Bouacca, Parbarat,, Helena and Morat, commonly known as the colony of Bay Islands, from their connection with our crown ; and, whereas, we have in furtherance thereof entered into a treaty with the Government of Honduras, by virtue of which the said islands are to be ceded to the said Republic ; now, therefore, having received information that the ratifications of the said treaty having been exchanged at Comayagua, know ye that we shall at, an early day. of which farther

notice will be given, proceed to cede the said islands to such commissioners as may be appointed by the President of the said Republic to receive them. Upon which cession our sovereignty iu and over the said colony will cease and determine. And our loving subjects and other inhabitants of the Bay Islands will now take notice thereof, and govern themselves accordingly. Witness, His Excellency Thomas Price, E-q., Lieutenant-Governor of the said Colony of Buy Islands, this the twenty-first day of May, in twenty-tbird year of our reigu, Aunoque Domini, one thousand eight hundred and sixty. » x « e e 8 x a. y i. » , NOTES ON COMETS. 100. What are those comets which traverse the solar system in vast eccentric orbits ? Are they oceans isolated in space ? And because ol this is a comet with an eccentric orbit a solid, or a mass of ice as it traverses the region of its aphelion? Is it a liquid as it nears the sun, and is it a vapour as it moves in the region of its perihelion ? And is it so, that a portion of that vapour from its proximity to the sun is resolved into steam and thus becomes invisible? After the perihelion passage has taken place, and during the comet's recess from the sun, is the portion of that vapour, which from its proximity to the sun had become transparent, again by a reduction of temparature made visible, and during the comet's further recess from the sun is the vapour, from a still greater reduction of temperature, condensed into a liquid, and thus the comet without a tail and without a nebulous atmosphere presents itself as a star of inferior magnitude þÿ a bright, concentrated point? Sir John Herschel, in his observation on Ilal ley's comet, which made its appearance in 1835, states, that on the evening of the 28th of October, before the termination of the twilight, he obtained ail excellent view of Hal ley's comet, eighteen days previous to its perihelion passage; its appearance was about that of a star of the third magnitude, which, as the darkness increased, appeared somewhat hazy. In a night glass the tail 3 in length was conspicuous. After the perihelion passage had taken

place, Sir John Herschel observed that the comet was actually increasing in dimensions and with such rapidity that it might almost he said to be seen to grow. (The increase in the dimensions of comets in their recess from the sun was pointed out by M. Valz.) In the comet's further recess from the sun the continued dilatation of the comet was observable. Sir Sohn Ilerscliel says, "I can hardly doubt that the comet was (airly evaporated in perilielio by the heat and resolved into transparent vapour, and is now in process of rapid condensation and reprecipitation on the nucleus. During the comet's retreat from the sun the tail began to be developed. The nucleus became more bulky, hazy, and ill defined, and its tail was strong, which afterwards gradually and Henceforward the comet presented the appearance of a round nebula, highly and very suddenly condensed in ilie middle, which gradually died away until finally lost. M. Boguslawski, professor of astronomy, sixty days after the perihelion passage, actually observed the comet as a star of thesixth magnitude þÿ a bright concentrated point. 101. Is it not so, that the impact of a comet upon our world is possible; and when we reflect upon the number of comets which traverse the solar system whose aphelion passage is beyond that of our planet, but whose perihelion passage is within the earth's orbit, þÿ is it not so, that the impact of a comet upon our world is probable? Moreover when we consider the ages that have rolled on during the past history of

our world, and the countless numbers of comets which have traversed the solar system during that period, and when we reflect that a comet within a given distance of our planet is less attracted towards the 6un than towards the earth, þÿ is it not so, that the impact of comets upon our world must have been inevitable? 102. If the impact of comets upon our world during its past history must have been inevitable, and a comet which traverses the solar system is an ocean isolated in space, is it so that our world has derived its ocean from the visitation of eometa?

103. But what are those comets, the disco\ ery of which was made by Encke and Biela? Are they portions ofthe atmosphere of that planet which by a "cosmical convulsion," is supposed to have burst into fragments ; and is it so, that other portions of that atmosphere and other fragments of that planet are still in reserve for future discovery ? 104. If a comet which, in its course of revolution about the sun, traverses the solar system, becomes a solid, a liquid, and a vapour, þÿ will more of the sun's rays be intercepted by it when it is a solid or a liquid, than when it is a vapour, and more when it is a vapour than when, from its proximity to the sun, it is resolved into steam and becomes invisible? and is it because the mass of a comet in its course of revolution about the sun never varies, but the impulsion of the sun's rays upon it vary, that the comet's orbit is eccentric ? 105. If those comets which circulate about the sun in vast eccentric orbits are oceans isolated in space, would the impact of a comet upon our world be a force adequate to produce t hose phenomena which are presented to us in the formation of the boulder clay ? According to geologists, the boulder clay formation appears to emanate from a common centre, and owes its origin to no ordinary operations ot water. It consists of accumulations ol sands, gravel clays, and boulder stones, huddled up in the same indiscriminate mass, without regard to sedimentary deposition, or to gravity, or to any ot her law of arrangement.

Is it from this cause : Matter ceases not to be projected front the sun, the momentum of which is such, that as it impinges upon the nebulous atmosphere which surrounds the nucleus of a comet, that atmosphere, during a comet's approach to the sun, is impelled behind and beyond the nucleus; whereas, when the comet recedes from the sun, the matter which is'projected from that body, impels the atmosphere to extend in advance of the nucleus? þÿ Notes for enquiry on the sciences of Geology and Astronomy, by Charles Chalmers.

I have felt it the more incumbent upon me to treat of this important matter, because ot my self-imposed, though ungrateful, task of trying to expose to the people and submit to the judgment of their common sense, our existing institutions, the laws regarding them, aud tie deviations and abuses of these laws; and I can assure the Public, that, although in general, laws are not treated with much re-pect in this Island, yet none have been and none are more abused and set aside, than those enacted with a wise anil kind forethought for tile expeditious furthering of Dealings, and the safety of their property. I must, however, make honorable mention of our ordinary Healing-Courts as they are at present, which, if not in all respects as efficacious and off-hand as they might he easily made to he, arc at least regardful of the laws, acting in view of their responsibility, and hon- in estly caring tor and preserving the means their trust, more than can be said of many Exe-

cutors, under whose management Dealings have been protracted ad infinitum , and their property squandered, lost and eat up by the executors, as most ol us have seen, and as every one who will open his eyes can see to this very day. Dealingcourts, so called from the Danish word for dividing (dele, skifte), because of their task to divid estates among heirs or creditors, arc Institutions of very ancient origin in Denmark. By the Code of King Chiistian V, the Institution was properly defined, and rules enacted for the guidmeenf the functionaries appointed to administer and divide Dealings, and who were in that Code 5-2-90 denominated Dealingmasters (Skiftefoi valtere ) and were given a certain jurisdiction, so that their function was both a judicial and an administrative one, their decisions in the firstnamed capacity being subject to appeal to a sup. rior Court, whereas their find ings in then second capacity could be redressed only upon a complaint to a higher magisterial authority At first these Dealingmasters were limited in their functions to the administration and division of intestate Estates, while all other kinds ol divisions of pioperty amongst heirs or creditors were li ft to the private arrangemnta of those concerned ; but in time, with the expansion of society and the spread of wealth consequent upon the development of agriculture, trade and industry, the Dealingcourts were also developed and amplified, and came at last to embrace all kinds of Estates and Dealings,

while the legislation thereupon gradually followed and legalized the extent of spheie and action into which the Institution had expanded. Thus, by the word þÿ þÿDealing is now understood, all such administrations and divisions of property, which, either according to law or at the request of parties concerned arc held and done by the Dealingmasters, ordinary or extraordinary. in these Colonies the Dealingcourts have undergone much change as to their formation and composition, oven more titan in Denmark, and, it is very remarkable, that every change has been expressly enacted for the sake of a better control, and to prevent the recurrence of detected abuses. The following synopsis will best show the manner in wbioh the Institution has boon developed here. 1, The Royal Ordinance of 31st March 1755 concerning the administration of Justice and

Police in the three Islands, enacts, that the Dealings are to be held in each town by the town-judge and the recorder, together with two solvent pe rsons appointed by the secret Council, all of whom are responsible for the meaus belonging to the Estates and to the minors. 2, The Royal Ordinance of 17th Nov. 1779 for St. Croix, which abolishes the then existing two Dealingcourts, and institutes one single such Court for the whole Island, composed as follows : the law-member of the Royal Council, the town-judge of Christiansted, the town-judge of Fredeiiksted, and a special Dealingmastef ; and further two sworn Kingsclerks, and the necessary writers. 3, The Royal Ordinance of 6th Dec. 1799 for St. Croix, by which the two Dealingcourts are re-established, each consisting of two members, viz : the town-judge of each jurisdiction and a special Dealiugmnster. 4, The Royal Ordinance of 17th April 1807 for St. Thomas and St. Johns, establishing a Dealingcourt for St. Thomas composed of two members, one of whom is the Notary public and the other a specially itpja i . d I) alingmaster; and ordaining that the judge in Sf Johns shall continue as hitherto to aci as Dealingmaster. The collection of debts due to (lie Dealings were according to special enactun nts entrusted to the respective lncassatois to the Biwglui- Councils, except in cases where a nifietilar Incassator had been appointed for an espi ci < 1 Dealing. 'i'lte appointment of a man with the ability and experience of local affairs as Counselor Birch to be at the head of our Government, cannot hut give gemtal satisfaction ; and we have heard, on all sides, great hopes ntei ta in- ( d of the benefit to be derived to these Colonies from ltis administration.
