(Continued.) 1, by Gov. þÿHansen sOrdinance of 28th Jan. 1849, it was enacted that the Burgher-Councils or their Incassators should no longer collect the claims due to Dealings, but that these collections should devolve upon tiie Deal ugcourts ; 2, by the ltoyal Ordinance of 14th Aug. 1850, the preceding enactment was sanctioned, adding rules and instructions to be observed by the Dealingcourts with respect to collections and their deposits in the State-treasury, ordaining that no Dealiugmaster shall keep a larger sum in hand than $300, and that ho shall make a monthly report to Government of the amount of cash in hand ; 3, by a ministerial resolution of Sept. 1855, by which the existing separate Dealingcourts were abolished, and the judge of each jurisdiction was appointed as Dealingmastur in addition to his other functions. Thus, the result of these changes is that there are no longer separate Dealingmastersjn these Islands, but that the judge iu encli jurisdiction is also Dealiugmaster therein ; that each Dealingcourt has only one member ; that the Dealingmaster is Incassator to the Dealings ; and that their means must be deposited iu the Statechest. In how far those changes have acted beneficially, or otherwise, the time lias been too short as yet to prove ; it seems, however, that every enactment quoted above purported a stricter control and the prevention of serious abuses, consisting not only in mismanagements, but defalcations and embezzlements ; whereas the later

enactments have nearly abolished all control. One of them in particular seems to me to have been adopted not only without a sufficient reason, but even with great temerity, viz : the abrogation of the Burgher-Councils function as Iucassator. It will probably be remembered, that upon the cession of this function, the Bur-

ST. P;&Oj()I t \N S gher-Counci! of this Island found that, there was not sufficient occupation for a separate Incassator to the Council, and that they therefore merged this office into one with the office of Secretary and Bookkeeper, thereby saving part of the þÿIncassator salary, s or rather, saving the 4 per cent, fee upou collections to Dealings, by which this Incassator was paid. This saving is, however, merely imaginary, as the Dealingcourts have to pay the same, and often even a higher, commission for their collections. But the measure, besides exempting the þÿBurgher-Council s Incassator from all control, by making the same person Secretary, Bookkeeper and Incassator, has likewise done away with nearly all control upon the collections in Dealings, and tends to expose their means to much risk of being lost. For, the Dealingmaster has many other occupations besides, and can give only a small part of his time to the details of a number of Dealings, and, what is worse, he is not subject to the same obligation and responsibility in this respect as the former Incassator was. 1 shall, iu order to elucidate the matter, briefly stale how i formerly btood according to the laws above quoted. The Ordinance of 3ist March 1755 laid the responsibility for all propeity belonging to Dealings and Minors, upon the lour members then composing the Dealingcourt, and also upon the Government-Council for the property of Minors. By the þÿKing sRescript of 19th Oct. 1770 all collections for Dealings should in general devolve

upon the Burgher-Council, who were joiutly lesponsible for the collections, and wete allowe d a percentage thereon. By the þÿKing Rescript s of 4th Nov. 1778 thfe law for Denmark of 30th Oct. 1767 concerning collections for Dealings was extended to these Islands. This law enacts, þÿ that whereas some Dealingmaster s have appointed themselves or others as Incassators without consent of the heirs, and thereafter delayed the Dealing in order the lunger to keep its money, þÿ it shall depend upon the heirs, their attorneys or guardians to appoint an Incassator; and strictly forbidding the Dealingmaster to make any such appointment, except on (lie request of all the heirs. The Ordinance of 17th Nov. 1779 for St. Croix, intimates that as there had hitherto been great delays in the closing of Dealings, it is enacted that there shall be only one Dealingcourt in the Island, þÿ in which everything is to he so arranged, that the Dealings can be expedited and closed without delay, and not postponed any longer than extremely þÿnecessary. ' The Ordinance then renews the enactment of the Rescript of 19th Oct. 1770 about the collections to be effected by the Burghef Council. The þÿKing Rescript s of 19th Aug. 1791, concerning t lit- Uppercuuit ami Burgher-Council of St. Thomas, as well as the collections to Dealings in all the Islands, enacts in this latter respect, that the Burgher-Councils shall be the Incassators to all Dealings, and that the moneys collected shall be deposited with the said Coun-

cils ; that the Dealingcourts shall with the utmost speed make out lists of the debtors to the respective Dealings, summon the debtors to appear at the fixed sessious of the Couits to acknowledge their debt, and hand the lists to the Burglmr-Couneil or its Incassator for collection of the debt. The Burgher-Council was responsible for the amount, unless they proved that they had sued the debtors within six weeks I after receiving the claim for collection. Finally, the Dealings or Estates had a preferable tight against the Burgher-Council, and its members in solidttm, for their means entrusted to i them, and enjoyed the same privilege as the State-treasury according to D. L. 5 þÿ 14 þÿ 37 holds with regard to the þÿKing collectors s And the Burgher-Council had a preferable right, a mortgage-right, against their Incassator and his estate for all sums entrusted to his collection.
